At Wills Coffee house I did take the Duke of Argile aside and told him I had writ you some account of the Debates of the Lords upon the Spainish affairs and among other things I had writ that the Duke of M- had reckoned your Regiment as one that was taken from the Flanders establishment and had never been made up to him, and that you had not writ to him to tell him the manner it was made up, because you did not know but I might have made a mistake in what the Duke of M- said. The Duke of Argile told he remember very well the Duke of M- did say so, and that he remember then he told him it was not then a proper time to answer him but when it was he could answer, the Debate then running upon the Deficiences at the battle of Almansor; and afterwards went and sat by him and told him of Cadogan, Ross, and Stairs troops coming over which made
up for your Regiment. Then he told me he knew very well how all that matter of your Regiment was managed, and he could have told the Duke another reason why he would not want any of his number, for the twelve pence in the pound he was to have. But that matter is all over, it is too late to talk of that now.

You'll see in the Gazett the account Capt. Cosby gives of our misfortune in Spain, but in his discourses in coffee houses he blames the Marshal more plainly, and some that have talked to him say he says he believes he let Stanhope be lost out of a Pique, not knowing the enemy was so numerous, and though he might have had a cheaper Victory over them.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, November 15, 1711.

I can now tell my Dearest life and soul that much to my satisfaction I am now settled in our house much better then I could have believed for the time we have had posseian of it, for Capt. Powell got all things as ready as he could before I cam to town. I am extremely pleased with the worked Bed, for now tic cleaned it is as good as new and looks very gentell. I have hung the room with green Camlet. I hope nothing will prevent my going over to you (for all the pleasures this world can aford me without your company I find do's not in the least divert me) and so the less furniture I put up the better (though to my great comfort they now talk of a peace again very much). I heard to-day that there is two french gentlemen com over in the ship with Madam Gouerneys daughter and are gone to the Queen to Hampton Court, who it is given out is very ill of the gout; and Lord Oxford it is also said is ill, but for reasons of State, and for the same reason the Parliament is adjourned. I fancy you'll think me very ridiculous to pretend to send you any news of this kind, but you bid me send you all the Chatter-Chitter I heard, so like an obedient wife I'll obey your commands; tho at the sam time I know my self a fool in sending you that for news that you knew before, but nevertheless to obey your commands I'll begin again. Count Gallass is leaving this Court very soon with the greatest disgrace in the world; it is said he is wholly wrapped up in the Whigg interest and so by consequence opposed the peace with the utmost rigour. If so I am so very angry at him I could ring his neck off, though I keep all those voiolent inclinations to my self. Lord Harley is very soon to marry the Duke of Newcastle's daughter. Mrs. Kingdom it is generally said is marred to Lord Conway, but it is not yet owned. Sister Wentworth gave a ball before she left Windsor. A lady told me yesterday that she was a making a visit to the Duchess of Shrewsbery and Sister W- cam in and the Duchess entertained
her with no other discourse but commending of me, and how glad she was you ware marred, that at last my sister was not very well pleased with the subject. I am told the Duchess of Marlborough intends to set up an Assembly to out do the Duchess of Shrewsberry's. I think myself the happiest person in the world and I hope our love to won another is so sinceire that that alone will crown all our other blessings in this world.

TEI.text: St. James's Square, November 20, 1711. I have this day been to see Lady North an Gray and made her all the fine specches I could think off, and have promised her to carry her to an Opera which she seemed very much pleased with; her cloths are not yet com, so I have not my scarf yet. I sent you word I was to go to Hampton Court last Sunday, which I did, but my father would have me take his coach horses and saddle horses for my men. The queen took a great deal of notis of me, and the Duchess of Somerset is most extremely civil to me, as soon as I cam (though she was not in waiting) engaged me to dine with her, and Lady Scarborough invited me to diner, but I was engaged before. The Duke of Marlborough went up the back stars to the Queen jest as I cam away. You desire scandal and this town at present will supply you, for Lady Linsey is with child and the town says if she knows the father it is Lord Lumley. Mrs. Grant (that was maid of honour) is going to bring her husband into Doctors Commons for being akin to Lord Sharrard. Lady Guilford is mad. I hope you wont now complain for Scandal. I am a torment to every body that comes near me for Ballets but can get non. Lady Batthurst and that family makes the greatest court in the world to me. Lord Barkley has been twice to see me but I was not at home.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James Square, November 23, 1711.
My dearest life and soul,

I am now to thank you for my hood and scarf which without a compliment is the finest I ever see; Lady Wentworth is ten times more delighted with it than if you had sent it to her self. Mrs. Robinson has been with me to-day and I would make her drink tea. I find she is very much transported at his being Plenipotentinary , but she says those things called pages she's most concerned at, for they are what she has never been used to, but when they have don with them she'll make them all parsons. She and I am the best conversation in the world, for I am very grave with her, and whatever she says I conferm she is infinitely in the right. Here is no news nor scandal stirring that is new. I have here sent you the Spectators for Mr. Elleson said you had them always sent to you, and I have them taken in, so the same will do. I can say no more for Lady Wentworth is staying in pain for this letter for fear she should not be time enough to writ her self; I tell her I'll asure you she and all her little family of creatures are well and so she need not write this post, but that will not do. I am my dearest life and soul yours entirely.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Hampton Court, November 23, 1711.
Dear Brother,

Being misinform my self last Tuesday I misinform you, for it seems notwithstanding the General report Mr. St. John was never designed to have been a Plenipotentiary, when I told it Mr. L- for news, he said, it might be but he could not believe it, it would be using Prior hardly that had the Management with Monsr Manager, when he was named by the French for one of their side, not to name him of ours; and he yesterday told me he heard Mr. Prior would be the third. The Queen goes to morrow for London, and I hope
will convince them that she has not been in that dangerous condition that some disaffected people has been pleased to report her. There came in a fellow booted and spurred to a coffee house in the City Sunday night and said he was just come from Hampton Court, and the Queen was given over. She has been a broad these two or three days and I thank God very well. Mr. Lewis told me yesterday that they sent a messenger that day to Holland. If I had been in London, I would have sent you some of the Prints that have been published about the disign'd procession of Queen Elizabeth's birth day. The figures that were taken are showed at the Cock-pit, and I hear the Duchess of Marlborough has been to see them. The Duchess of Montague and Lady Sunderland went their in a Mob, to have past for Servant Maids, but every body knew them. They say the Duchess of Marlborough designs this Winter to keep assemble`es and live after a most magnificent manner at her new house, but I think she might be warned by the advise she had from a country Gentleman of about two hundred a year, who was made very drunk at her house at St. Albans, for it seems she has kept open house there all this summer; he told her, her entertainment was very noble and fine, and if she had lived so two or three years ago it might have signified something, but now it would signify nothing. We hear here the place of Congress is Utrect, and the time the first of January, our stile, and it is expected that you will have more Volunteer at that Congress then ever you had at any Campaign. There has been a report that you would have time before the meeting of the Plenipos to come into England but now I find there's no thoughts on it. I was t'other day in company with Lord Steward and heard him say it was to be wished you could have time to appear here this Session, if it were only upon the account to leave your Proxy, for the Party in the house of Lords were much stronger then in the house of Commons. This is a place I hear very little news, and when I come to London where I fancy I shall hear more, I may be disappointed; but since you have encouraged me you shall not fail of hearing constantly from your, &c.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, December 4, 1711.
I could freely live all the year round in a desert with only you, and say with a great sinceirity
I would not envy kings there state
Nor once desire a happier fate.

I'm afraid you'll think I am turned poet. Lady Pawlet and I am very well together and Lady 'Stiffback' in her formal way. I am to day to go to a very od figure of a Lady that's Lord Treasurer's who is like an old house keeper, but I hear Lord Treasurer takes it as a compliment paid to him for she seldom goes a broad, so I am content'd to do it in hopes it may be of service to you. I last week met the Duchess of Marlborough and the Duchess of Mountague in a viset and they both looked upon me with the most spleen and mallis I ever see people. I own I think they may envy me but I envy nobody, for as you and I love won another all things else in this world are but Trifles. I believe sister Wentworth is now more extravagant then ever for fear the
world should think she is mortified at your being marred, but she can't govern her passions so much but the world takes notis of her uneasiness. She is talked on for Mr. Nash and Coll. Joslain more then ever. I wonder her husband can be so imposed on as to be pleased with there company. She is mighty witty as she thinks upon Capt. Powell. I own I like sister Betty's humour very well, I carry her abroad with me very often; I can't but say I think my carring her into good company might be of advantage to her and make her gentell which indeed at present she is not. I have now sent you two Ballets. As for scandal the town has now a great deal at Lady Mary Gore's cost, though some says she deserves more then is said of her. At the Bath there was a particular set of company six men and six women that met two or three times a week to dance, and won night all the candles was blown out, and the men was very rude, upon which Mr. Gore desired her to go no more into that company, but she told him she would and if citizens pretend'd to marry Quality they must take it for their pains. And Lord and Lady Berkley has had a great quarrel about one Capt. Smith's wife. When I here of all these Quarrels I think how happy I am in having won I love and loves me again. Lord Barkley has been three times to see me, and I have happened to be always abroad which I was very sorry for. The Queen has changed her Drawing room nights to Tusdays and Fridays, to night is the first she has had since she cam to town; I go with Lady Portland. The Duke of Kent is made a Jest on by every body in being (as he thinks) the head of the Whigg Party, for sure never any body was so free as he is; he subscribed considerably to those Images that made such a noise. I believe his ready money is no great Burden to him, he need not be so free of it. The Bookseller need not send you any more Spectators for I'll do it, being always desirous to be of use to you. These verses was sent to Lord Treasurer.
Though Guiscard's knife mistook the Stroke
Felton's sword may do the work.

note.value: FROM LADY ISABELLA WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: December 7, 1711.

My dearist and best of children, I was yesterday att Lord Keeper's, I went with dear Lady Strafford, who is hear now,
but thear is Lady Evling Pirpoynt, and Lord Sherwood's sister, and more young ladies, so I have stole from them to make myself and them much esier, and to give myself the pleasure of conversing with the Darling of my soul, who it is a pleasure to think of when absent. I hope Mr. Powel is arrived safe with you. They say thear is a ship lost, that came over with the Duke of Ormon. Its sad the Duke of Molberry was put out of a place worth three thousand a year, and has laid down that in the Army. Thear are abundance of stories go about, but one very commical it is that Dockter Gath went to Lord Darkmuth and told him he was sorry he must go to law with him for breaking open his house taking his goods out. So my lord asked what he meant; he said the house where the images was taken from was his, and the Devil was his. My lord said he would return the Devil to him again. The Dr. said he designed to make a great funurel for the Devil and have a sermon preached. My lord asked what the tex should be; he said it was, that his desyples came in the night and stoal him away. Pearl is groan very fat but dus al her Tricks and is very Brisk. Lady Wentworth is to bring her Dogs to vesitt mine - and mine must not be so ill bred but return the vesitt. Bell went to-day to see Lady Limster and my lord was just then given over by the Dockters. I think it is a very unholsom season one day is a great frost next very hot. Thear is hoops for you yett, the Twelve thousand pt. lot is not yet drawn. Dear Soul I fear I have teared you, therefore I will ad no more then to asure you I am your most infinite affectionate Mother.
Millions of thancks to my dear soul for all your cair of me.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, December 11, 1711.
Dear Brother,

There was some people of opinion that the vote of the house of Lords might be retrieved the next day, but I hear all the ministry was not entire of that mind, so it was not pust in earness. Lord North and Grey opened the debate and said he could not tell whether it was very regular, but he hoped since what had happen in the house of Commons was sufficient for them to think of some expedient to alter what had past their house yesterday by so small a majority as one. I believe he was surprised to find so long a Pause after his speech, and that when Lord Jernsey that had voted with him the day before declared that though he had voted that the advise that was given should not stand part of the address, but now it was carried by a majority it was not Parliamentary, when they thought they had mustered up more of their opinion, to endeavour to alter it. Then some lords desired if it was to stand part of the address, that they might have the liberty to protest, and it was answered readily, yea, yea; then the Speaker said "is it your pleasures that this advise stands part of your address," and the noise for the affirmative was
greatest, then the Keeper said "the yeas have it, let it be ordered." My Lord Anglesea rise up and desired the question might be put, whether that should stand part of the address. The Lords of the other side said no such question could be put after once the Keeper had said let it be ordered. My Lord Anglesea insist'd that till the Keeper had said "as many as are content, say content, and as many as are not, say not content," and this saying "yeas have it," without divideing the house would not do, whilst there was any Lord would say he had said no. My Lord Rivers, Lord Carmarvene, said they had said no, upon which the house divided. They that were for having the advise part of the address was ordered without the bar, and they that staid in the house saw they would loose several they had the day before, cried yield, the others cried tell, tell, so that for some time there was a great noise in the house. The Keeper appointed two tellers, Lord Abington and Lord Sunderland; Lord A- would not tell because those of his part said yield, Lord Sunderland said if he did not do his duty he would his, and tell without him, and so begun. But they that would not be told hoped and skipped about, which was sport for us that were spectators. The house of Commons was up soon that day, so there was a great many; which made some Lords appoint that the orders of their house might be read in order that nobody should come into the house but Lords, which was read a Monday. The Queen has showed her liking of the Commons address better then the Lords by ordering them to attend her first, the dissenting Lords went with the Commons yesterday, and the address of the Lords was not so well attended as was expected to-day. But it is very doubtful what to make of this business for people know that my Lord T- to be a very adroit and able man do say he could not have been so out of his computation without some further fetch that we poor mortals can't dive into. They say the Duke of Somerset, just by the Queen, call out louder for the question then anybody, and was not only content with that and a proxy he gave that way, but pulled out the Duke of Cleveland with him; and yet he keeps his place.

TEI.text:
St. James's Square, December 28, 1711. I love Lady Wentworth better than ever, for she is to me as if she ware my own mothere and I believe next to you she loves me the best. I have heard an old saying there is no catching old birds with chafe, so I hope I am to old for sister Wentworth to play me any of her tricks, though I must say she has laid as many trapps to draw me into her gang of company as ever any body did; but she has never accomplished her design, for I have been but twice to see her since I cam to town and then I did only make her a formal viset. She has invited my sisters and I to play at cards with her of twelve day, and since I here there is to be Mr. Nash and a great many more of her fellows, so I don't intend to say any thing tell the day comes, and then I'll send her word I have a great cold and so can't wait on her. I am not so much a fool but I can see through her designs, for she thinks if she introduces all her folks to me, if the world reflects on her for keeping such company, she'll say that I keep there company as well as she. I think my brother the greatest fool that ever was, for he is the fondest thing of the world of Nash and delighted with all his wife dos. She cam to the Queen's Chaple last Sunday after the prayers ware over, and she and Lady Jersey sat out among the men, which was made a great jest on; but my brother seemed mightily pleased at her contrivance and said she was much in the right, it was the warmest place. The Queen is still ill of the gout and a cold; I go to the back stars every day to know how she dos, for the
lady in waiting always tells who comes to know how she dos. One of your tickets is a blank, the other is not yet come up. I have four blanks and two 20 l. and two to com up; if I have the 12,000 l. it is at your service, as my self is and every thing else is I have. I hear the Queen will not consent to have the Duke and Duchess of Somerset removed. I hear there is a most scandalous Lampoon com out against the Duchess of Somerset, but I have not seen it, for I am very cautious who I inquire for things of that nature of, and perticalarly of her, because the whole family is so civil to me.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: January 6, 1712.

It is a new world since I had the honour to write to you, the D. of Marl. out of all his places, the D. of Ormond in some of them, twelve new Lords, at which some take offence, others laugh, though no body can deny their being well chosen, at least most of them, for their estates and families.

They will have it that the D. of Somerset is to be out, but I doe not hear it is so yet. Her Grace looks melancholy, as I think she hath reason. I find P. Eugene will come in spite of the world, but his journey is not like to signify much unless some people here hope by his means to raise the mob. It is reported that D. Hamilton is to be Master of the horse, but I am apt to think that story proceeds from himself, as that of his being Secretary of State last Summer. They say he and his country men have made an address to the Queen, about their being excluded the house of Lords, and that they flatter themselves with bringing that matter over again, but it is to be hoped that cannot be done. The Queen saw company on new year's day, where I had the honour to see My Lady Strafford. My Lord Windsor hath at last attained to what he hath so long desired, but how a man of his singularity likes coming in with so much company, your Lordship knows better then I doe. Now you are entered upon your great business, I shall be afraid of writing, unless it be to put you in mind now and then of your Lordship's most humble and most obedient Servant.

note.value: FROM LADY ISABELLA WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, January 8, 1712.

My dearist and best of children, a thousand thancks to you for the kindness of yours of the 12 of this instant, but I shall never think it possible for any dog to compaer to charming Pearl, I never go anywhere without her except to church. Hear is a strange unnatural report of Lady Abargane that she has in potion kilt her own child about seven year old, she having been a great while whipping it, my Lord being greeved to hear it cry so terryably went into the room to beg for it, and she threw it with such a force to the ground she broack the skull; the girl leved but four hours after it. I am sure never any letter from me was half so welcome as this will be, although I never will yield that any creature can lov you better then, dear soul, your most infinite affectionate mother.

note.value: P.S. IN LADY STRAFFORD'S HANDWRITING
TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Lady Wentworth tells me you are very fond of folly, I am glad of it believing you will grow fonder than ever of me sense Folly has your Affection. I have taken it into my head that Prince Eugene has been some time or other wounded in the -, for I never see any body sit down so stiff. I here the Whiggs are very angry with you, I think it is for you credit, for they never love any body that is good. I am my dearest Life and Soul more then I can express my self yours intirly.

TEI.text:
St. James's Square, January 8, 1712. Prince Eugene was with the Queen a Sunday night, Mr. St. Johns went with him. I hear he is very much mortified at the Duke of Marlborough being out of favour. The Duke of Shrewsbury is still named for Ireland, his Duchess is very ill of a feavore. I go to day in all my aires to see the Prution envoy's lady, and the Ds. of Buckingham sees
company, so design to go there to-night. I hear Mr. Prior is discontented and dos not think the court dos well by him. I was told to-day that the Queen will not consent to have ethere the Duke or Duchess of Somerset taken from her.
I sent you word in the beginning of this that the Queen was to have a Drawing room to night for Prince Eugene; but she has a little of the gout, so she had non. But I went to make a viset to the Duchess of Ormond, and Prince Eugene cam to make her a viset, so she told him who I was. Jack How's son has run away with Mrs. Thynn, Lord Weymouth's niece. I am jest com from the Prution Envoy's lady, she is handsome, but her face is exactly like a sign in the Strand where they sell Babies; she cant speak a word of English, she told me she se you at the Hague.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, January 12, 1712.
Dear Brother,

The Whigs are pleased to give out that there was but very odd figures at Court of the Birthday, and that there was no Women fit to look at but my Lady Strafford, Lady Lansdown, and Lady North. They gave out before that there would be very little company, and it was said the Queen would not come out; but there was as much fine clothes as ever, and I thank God the Queen appeared both morning and afternoon as usual, and the next day had got no cold but was rather better then before, and a friday I was out with her to take the air in Hide Park. On her Birth day she gave P- E- a sword set with diamonds, the Queen being to be carried in her chair from her dressing room to the great Drawing
room, everybody but the ladies in waiting and my Lord Chamberlain was kept out of that apartment; but when the Queen goes in her chair it is my business to be there, so I saw my Lord Chamberlain come in with P- Eugene alone and go into the dressing room, and after staying 2 or 3 minutes he came out with the Sword the Queen had given him in his hand, and then pulled off his own Sword and gave it to a page of the back stairs that stood at his elbow, and put on t'other.

There was better order kept this birthday then ever I saw, at night the Guards were doubled, some people affirm there was no occasion for it, but only to show their diligence and over and above care, and to cast an odium upon some people, but other people that pretent to know more say it was no work of supperrogation but what was absolutely necessary.

It was talked of as if the Duke of M- intended to make a ball that night at his house, but when he found how it was took as a sort of vying with the Court, he let it alone, but the Duchess of Marlborough did send to several Ladies to invite them to a dancing a friday night. I know some ladies she invited, but that morning there was papers cried about the Street as representing it a design to set up for themselves, that there was several people that had made cloth for that day that had not for the birthday; so they put off their Ball but sent to all the Ladies they had invited there would be no dancing but that the Duchess would be at home, and should be glad to see any of them that would come. The Queen was at the house a Saturday and past three public Bills and my Lord Gore's, P- E- was in the house and all the lords had their robs on; and there I saw the Scotch Lords, who has given out they will go to the house no more, and they say they went then purely out of respect to the Queen. In the Private cause between lord Moon and Duke Hambleton there was none of them there, the votes were equal, so proxies being called for Lord Moon cried it by 3. Yesterday I hear most of them was in the house and there was a great debate whether the Scotchs should be heard by Counsil before the Bill for toleration of Epicopacy be read, which is sent up by the house of commons; it was carried that counsel should be
heard on Wednesday, that is to morrow, so I intend to attend this house that day, for whilst counsel is at the bar they that can crowd may hear.

I have been told by those that were members of the house of commons at the time the Union was treated of that that matter was fully debated, and a toleration insisted on for the Episcopacy by the Archbishop of York's son with a great many reasonable arguments; but he was told by the members for Scotland that the Episcopacy there was better then if they had any such bill, for there was no law against them in Scotland, and a toleration would suppose they lay under the misfortune of being against the laws in being, and there was liberty for them to preach and pray as they pleased, so that they took the oaths to the Government. Then it was Mr. Sharp's business to show them a law against them, which he did as he thought by producing their Statute book, where any minister that should read the Liturgy of the church of England to a congregation forfeit so many marks for the first offence, and for the second or third Banishment; but that was proved by the Scots to be meant only against their own Ministers of the Kirk, and so looked upon by the house. So the business fell and is now revived out of a mischievous intention to the peace of the kingdoms, or by those whose Zeal is more predominant then their prudence. As far as I hear of this Bill there's no occasion to make such a noise about it one way nor t'other.

Whiteman's lieutenant Coll. writs that he's affair his men will have their throats cut in their beds. The Scotch Guards and some other Scotch regiments are sent for here and others are to go from hence in their room. If we had but once a good Peace we should be better able to deal with these sort of people.

I am pleased to hear the discourse continues that the Master of the horse is kept for you. I was told by a lord that another Lord told him when he asked for it he was answered it was kept for you, and that I heard again by another, and Dr. English told me but yesterday that he had it from very great men, that you would certainly have it, though
the town reports it is either for you or the Duke of Argile, but he's pretty sure it is not designed for him, it is not yet put into commission. I have seen of late Sir Stephen Fox go often to the Queen, which was the only thing that given me an opinion such a commission might be. I was told a story to day which I will not affirm for truth till I have inquired farther into it. It was that a Gentleman desired to speak to the Queen, and the Duchess of Ormond being in waiting would have introduced him, but she was told by the page of the back stairs, that the Duchess of Sommerset was just gone and had left orders that nobody should be permitted to speak to the Queen till she came again. It is certain the Duchess of Somerset remains in great esteem with the Queen still. My Lady Masham is not yet declared lady of the Bedchamber, lady Katherine Hide has waited as such. The day before the birth day I was to know if the Queen would go abroad; she would not go out but bid me have the chair in readiness the next day, so I found I could not avoid being seen by her and my cloth not being come from Holland I took up a resolution to make a plain suit and was telling my Lady Burlington my disappointment, who told me she knew several in my case &c., but when she went abroad with the Queen she told her all I had said to her, so that my compliment was better made to the Queen, then if I had not been disappointed. It was very obliging of Lady Burlington for which I tell you the story. I wish I had my money again, let who would have the clothes.

There's five mails come in and I have just now received the favour of four Letters from you of 5th, 9th, 12th, 16th. And when I go out I shall be flock't about for news. Before I came in I went into St. Jameses coffee house and there they said the french had explained themselves upon their proposals and that we should have canidy, Hudson's bay, and the same trade in the West indies as we had in the time of King Charles the 2nd; Dunkirk should be demollish't, but the Emperor was to renounce all his pretensions to the Kingdom of spain, and the Spanish flanders, but was to have Naples and some other places in Italy, Lisle and Douay to be restored to the
French, and there they shook their heads and more when they said the Elector of Bavaria and Cologne were to be restored. They run on with forty things more which were invented upon the coming of the Messengers, for the Mails were not yet come to town. They asked me, I told them I knew nothing for I had not my letters. I had heard you and others say before you sent me a copy of the Pentonary letter that you was very well with him, and therefore I did with a great deal of courage affirm it to be a lye and made story; and shall take care that nobody shall see any of your letters but to whom it may be of service to you. That I may not make your packet too big I must beg the favour of you to tell Mr. Powel I have received three letters from him, and thank him for the trouble I have given him, but I hear nothing of my clothes. I am glad he has received the Bill and shall writ to him next post; I fear my clothes are lost because they had not a charge of them from you.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, January 18, 1712.

I fancy you and I could live very prettily at Twittenham by our selves in a rural romantic way; I must confess it would not be very much in the modern way of living, but that's no matter so long as we like it. The Duke and Duchess of Beaufort are the fondest of won another in the world, I fear it is to hot to hold. He's never out after seven a clock at night, and if he has any company he takes an opportunity to tell them they must be gon by that time; and if he comes home and the Duchess is abroad he sends all the town over to fetch her home to keep him company. Now I own I fancy people may love won another as well without making so great a rout. It was carred by a great majority for sending Mr. Walpole to the Tower; my father is very tight to the court party, which I am very glad of, he sate in the house of commons till almost past twelve a clock last night to give Mr. Walpole a helping hand to the Tower. The Queen has still the gout in both feet which makes people think she can hardly be well enough to go to the house a Monday.

note.value: PASSAGE OMITTED

text.p: I have used the utmost of my skill to make a Tory of Mr. Elleson, but in vain.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, February 8, 1712.

It is a hard task my Dearest life for me to be almost three weeks and not hear from you, though I hope to have a good
many letters together. I must tell you that it was allowed I had the most Jewels of any body there, and the Queen told me I was very fine and my cloths was very handsome; and I thought myself very handsome, I hope if you had seen me you'd have been of the same opinion. Mrs. Scarborough the maid of honour was marred to Sir Robert Jenkeson, they gave favours to non but the court, except myself. General Web's daughter is com in maid of honour in her room. I think I never knew anything so much talked of as your being to be master of the horse, and if it is put into commition brother Wentworth will be one. I hear Prince Eugene is turned Tory, and the Duke of Ormond is the person that has made a convert of him. I believe in a little time you'll hear sister Arundell is run mad with pride, for I never see any take so much state upon her in my life as she dos, and because she could not be as fine as I and go to Court on the Birth, all Lady Wentworth could say she would not com to se me dressed. And because she has no coach I offered to call to carry her to church, and a Sunday when I went she let me stay some time and sent word she had not slept well and so could not go; but as she is very great with Lady Massam I will be very civil to her. I doe love sister Betty very, and I really believe she loves me, and we make shift to romp together every day, but she always comes by the worst. I have no news to send you, so will torment you no longer than to tell you I am entirely yours.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, February 12, 1712.

Lord Massam and Lord Bathurst is named for being in the Commission of Master of the Horse, tell your Excellence comes home. The Duchess of Somerset told me a Sunday that no Body was so fine of the Birthday as I,
indeed it cost me a great deal of money. The town has made out a story of the Duchess of Shrewsbery and Lady Oxford. The Duchess of Shrewsbery told me of it, she says they will always make a story of her every year, but she likes this the best. They say she went to see Lady Oxford and she said, "Madam I and my Lord are so weary of talking Politics, what are you and your Lord?" and Lady Oxford sighed and said "she knew no Lord but the Lord Jehova," and the Duchess made answer again "Oh, dear! Madam, who is that? I believe it is won of the new Titles, for I never heard of him before."

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, February 15, 1712.

I believe, my Dear, Utricht produces more news than this place, though about three weeks ago there was a story about town that fritten'd me out of my wits; I did not sleep for three nights. It was that a letter of yours was intercepted going into France against the States of Holland, and that they had set a gaurd about the door tell they could send you in disgrace out of there country; and I kept myself in this fright longer than I need, for I would not ask people what they thought for fear they should think I believed it; and I looked like a thing dead, but I told every body I had a great cold and it lay mightily in my head. So your poor Pug has been in great cares about you, though not without all the reason in the world, for what ever is any concern to you is dubly so to me. My diamond necklace is now the finest as well as my earrings of any body's in town. I must tell you that I wish as much as you for your being Master of the Horse; but if we have it not we have more happiness than ten thousand in this town, which is our love to won another, which no body can take from us. Prince Eugene has given an order to six ladies and six men. The ladies are the four Marlborough daughters and the Duchess of Bolton and Lady Berkely. It is a medall - Cupped on won side with a sword in won hand and a fann in the other, and the other side is Cupped with a bottle in his hand with a sword run through it. And the motto's are in French which I dare not write to you
but the English is "won don't hinder the other." I desire you'll send me some more of those French paper, for I take a great deal of pains and have translated it all. I have sent you the Examiners; I thought you might like to have the set, so I got you all this year's and will send them to you every week, though I hope there will not be many before I am so happy as to see you.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, February 25, 1712.

I have no news for I think there is nothing talked of but the death of Prince Eugene's nephu. He died of the small pox, but most people says he had more destempers then won, and they say he never went to bed sober sense he came, and he was a great admirer of Ladies; besides they say Prince Eugene is not much troubled for him. I hear Lord Treasurer is very uneasy about the Duchess of Somerset or they say
she is more public in espousing the Whig interest then ever. The town says Lord North and Gray is very jealous of his Lady, though they say without a cause, for I never heard no harm of her. I am jest com from the Drawing room, and the queen spoke to me very civilly, and Lady Wharton stood jest by the Queen, and she reached across her to speak to me and took no notis of her, which pleased me very much.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: February 26, 1712.

It is no compliment when I tell your Lordship that my heart leaps at the coming in of every post when I see your seal, tho it proves only a circular, for all of them I return many humble thanks. I was yesterday to wait of My Lady Strafford who hath had a sore throat, but was very well again and in cheerful and agreeable humour, that I regret the time you loose from her. We are in great expectation of the next letters to hear of the proposals of the allies, which I hope will quell in some measure the angry humour reigning at present, and give a better opinion then is generally conceived of the peace, I mean among people that will be convinced, for those who like themselves for being out of humour, it is no matter what they think or say. Prince Eugene's nephew dyed yesterday morning of the small pox, or rather of drinking which threw him into it, for he fell in with the young debauches here, who kept him continually drunk. They say his uncle was not well satisfied with him, nor did honour him with any great share of his kindness. Having never had the small pox, he was persuaded to remove out of Leicester house, and to lye at the D. of Grafton's in my neighbourhood. I saw a little more of him on Sunday last then I had done, in a visit to a Lady, but found him as reserved, though better bred then any English man. They talk of his going away soon.

My Lord Pelham is dead of an Apoplexy and left his son I believe the richest heir in England; with what he had
before of the D. of Newcastle's estate he must have admirable talents from nature, if such a heap of riches so young let's him be good for anything. They talk of great news of my Lord Albemarle's burning the French Magazines. If it proves true such a train of misfortunes upon France may make your work the easier.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p:
I have this morning my Dearest life received yours of the 5th March. I am going to day to the Cock Pit to Lady Wentworth, it being visiting day. Prince Eugene leaves this town to-morrow. Capt. Sanders carrys him over, he was here to know if I wanted anything to be carried over. The
Whiggs have now invented a new story which is that you swear and Hecter at Lord Privy Seal, and fright him out of his wits, and make him your tool. I am told that Lord Treasurer and Lady Massam begins to be jealous of won another. It is now again talked of the Duchess of Somerset's being out; and the key is named for the Duchess of Ormond or Lady Rochester. Mr. Stratford the merchant is broke and they say what was his ruin he laid out vast sumes the peace would be conclud'd by such a time, which time being exspired he was forced to go of. General Merits the Duke of Marlborough's great friend has most of what he is worth in his hands. Sister Betty will be in love with Prince Eugene, let me say what I will, for she is a terrible Whigg.
P.S. Sis Betty and I am this moment in a great dispute which is handsomest, she or I; we both argue in behalf of our own persons. Forget I am that insipid thing your wife, and be an impartial judge.

note.value: FROM LADY ISABELLA WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: March 4, 1712.

My dearist and best of children, a million of thancks to you for yours of the 8th of this instant. I have six the pretyist puppies of Flirts that ever you see. Sir Harry Johnson is to have one, and Sir John Lake is to have another, and Fill Cary another. Thear was a dreadful fire the other day in Albemal Street, Sir William Windom's house burnt down; the Duke of Ormon stopped it from going farther, he worked as hard as any of the ordinary men and gave many ginneys about to incurradg the men to work hard. A made ran baerfoot and in her smock to Nothumbarlin house with the strong box of jewels and most of the plate, and al his writings are saved, yet he has lost above twenty thousand pt. Two poor maids jumped out of the windoe, and beat thear brains out; one was very pretty, and was put out only to improve her, a rich grocer's daughter in the city. They are
much more concerned for their servants then for al the other lossis. You know Bell Skinner went to Italy with Lord Shasbury and his Lady, they wear but just settled at Naples before my Lady and Bell Skinner fell out, and my Lord paid twenty ginneys for her passadg back, and writins drawn for the captain to set her safe at Bristoe, which is near cus Hanbury. My Lord is the best of husbands. Mrs. Skinner hard thear you was married to a great fortune; my Lord said he did know your Lady, and if she had not a fardin, she would be the best fortune in England, she was so good. Indeed I am of my Lord's opinion.

TEI.text:
St. James's Square, March 11, 1712 Here is nothing talked about but men that goes in parties about the street and cuts people with swords or knives, and they call themselves by some hard name that I can nethere speak nor spell; but a Saturday night coming from the opera they asalted Mr. Davenant and drew there swords upon him, but he took won of them and sent to the round house, but it is thought it was sombody that would have been known and they gave money and made their eskape, but what was the great jest about town was they said they had cut of his head of hare. Pray tell Capt. Powell that won of his dear
Mr. Harvey's sisters is to be marred this week to Sir Rich. Anderson, and the other stays for him. You accuse me of sending you no verses, but it is because I had non unless I made them my self or stole them out of some old book; though I have jest found some that I can justly repeat to you not doubting but you'll soon return them with some of your own making.
I think my poetry very extrodinary; as a reward I desire you'll send me some green tea, for mine is almost gon.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, March 21, 1712.

note.value: PASSAGE OMITTED

text.p:
We have at last got rid of Prince Eugene. I fancy you wont make so great a rout with him as was made hear. I believe Mrs. Marshall was very sorry to leave London so soon, for she seemed to like it very well. I think her pretty but awkward and simple; and her husband is the formallest disagreeable piece that ever was seen, though I am very ungrateful in saying all this, for they made the greatest rout with me in the world, and he cam the night before he went away to know if I had any service to you. I have been at Mr. Jervises to see our pickturs; I think he has mended them both extremely and has made yours a good deal taller and the robes are well of them both. The Queen has a Drawing room to-night, so I go as soon as I have dined to the Cock Pitt to wait on Lady W - and then I go to Court; and I have made sister Betty go, for I think there
is nothing will improve her so much as keeping the best company. To morrow here is an opera for Nicolina's benefit, I believe all the town will be there; Lady Dartmouth and I go together, and Mrs. Hill, Lady Massam's sister. I was to see Lady Massam two days ago, and she was not at home; but she cam to see me the next day, which for her was very much, for she has disobliged a great many this winter by not paying there visits, though she has all this winter when she was well com very often to see me. Sister Wentworth goes to the Bath next month with Mrs. Cornish. All the Twittenham ladies that are in town have been to see me, except Lady Humble, who can't bare the sight of me to think I have got what she so much admired. I have asked Lady W- a thousand times to carry me to see her , but she says not for ten pound, for she is a mighty good woman and she would not have her laughed at for the world. I must tell you my love to Lady Wentworth every day increases, and I may venture to say I believe hers to me dos not decrease, for it is impossible for her to be fonder of me then she is; nor is it possible for me to be so fond of any thing as I am of your dear self. Adieu!

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, March 25, 1712.

I hear the Duke of Argile makes the greatest protestations of friendship for you that ever was. My father is laid up with the gout: I believe I shall jumble my guts out between this and Russell street, for since my father has been ill I have gon every day. Here is a new play which has taken extremely called the distressed mothere. I had not seen it tell last night for I don't much love Traidys , but I think it's a very good won. Lady Massam is very ill and her son is like to dye. It is said the Duchesses of Somerset and Shrewsbery is at great difference with won another. I still am told you are to be Master of the Horse. I wish the Queen would make me a Lady of the Bedchamber. I wonder Lady Scarborough keeps her place, for Lord Scarborough opposes the Queen in every thing that's in his power with all the voiolence in the world. I fancy by this time you'll think I never
intend to cease tormenting you with my nonsense. I fancy every letter you have from me you find me out to have less wit than you thought before; but you have won thing for your comfort, which is, the less wit women has the better wives they make, so according to that rule you are a most happy man in your choice.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p:
I have your Lordship's before me of the 30th new stile, a day of great expectation, which hath failed us, like most things of this world, by the French not giving their answer. It hath been reported here that they had desired a cessation of arms, and to deliver Dunkirk and Namur immediately, the first of great importance, the other of very little (I only tell you what is said in the town) and that this is only to prevent the siege of Cambray, after which we may march to Paris, I am afraid as we did after taking Lisle and Tourney. The D. of Argyle is come in high praises of General Staremberg, with whom he agreed better then Stanhope did, and I find that Staremberg is the New hope? of the tories, in opposition to Prince Eugene, who they say is but a novice in comparison of Staremberg. He must without doubt be an extraordinary man to maintain himself in such a country, under so many disadvantages. Then his personal qualities must gain the love of every body, no gasconnades, no haughtiness, and a life fit for a religious house. Now to go from a camp to a more peaceable place, I may tell you that the Sheriff's bill is not in a likely way of passing, for after three days fruitlessly spent about it they have been forced to refer it to a private Committee, where in all probability it will draw in length, and come to nothing. The D. of Shrewsbury certainly goes for Ireland, after long aspiring to it. There hath happened an odd thing lately in that country in the North parts, where they let great tracts of land for feeding cattle, which are kept by a few shepherds, and the poor people enraged that they
could get no labour, nor place to dwell, have slaughtered above twelve thousand sheep and other cattle. My Lord Northampton is made constable of the Tower, and this day the bill of recruits passed by commission with two private bills. The Duke of Ormond talks of going next week.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, April 14, 1712.

note.value: PASSAGE OMITTED

text.p:
Here is won Lunn a goldsmith broke with six thousand pound of Mr. St. Johns and as much of Lord Lansdown's
money in his hands, which I think should make people very carfull of trusting to goldsmiths. The Duke of Ormond is still here but he is to go very soon. The Duchess of Shrewsbery is at present very happy, for Coll. Murry is come from Scotland with whom the town says she has an intrigue. She is in that as she is in all other things not in the common way; for last week in the Drawing room Coll. Murry cam in so she run to every body she knew. "Oh!" says she, "here is Coll. Murry, the town says I have an intrigue with him, so I should not give him any of my pretty kind eyes, but I will and smile upon him two." You desired all the Chitter Chatter I heard, so in obedience to your Excellence's commands I doe, though I write nonsense.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, April 8, 1712.

I wonder Mons. Marshall Eugene can talk of his great living here, for they had a very indiferent lodging in St. James Street, and the house was kept the nastiest I ever see a house, and used to stink of your favourite dish, onions, ready to kill me; and she sat in the first room with a cole fire and tallow candles, which I know was made a great jest on. And for her head I leave you to judge how much like mine it is when you see her, for I dress mine exactly the same as when you went. Pearl is very well again which I am very glad of, for it is not to be expressed the rout Lady W- made with it while it was sick. She brought it here every day in two little night gownds made fit for it, and its legs was put into sleves, that I had a great deal to do to keep myself grave, for her affliction was to great for me to laugh. Lord Biron's Lady is dead, tic said she died of a distemper her Lord gave her. It is said the Duke of Graffton is to marry Lady Bell Benwick. Now they say the Duke of Shrewsbery dos not go to Ireland, for if there is a peace the Duke of Ormond will go himself.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, April 15, 1712.

I'm sure you would be much diverted if you did but see how earnest Lady Wentworth is about getting Sir William Wentworth for sister Betty; and Lady W- called
me up in a corner to beg of me to commend him to sister Betty, and she says she makes no doubt but twill doe, for his eyes she says sparkled mightily at the sight of sister Betty; and she is as grave when she speaks of him, and in her thoughts the match is already made up. Lord Mohun now owns his marriage to Duck Griffin; I wonder he should give himself the trouble to marry her, for every body says he has for some years taken the same liberties he can doe now. Sister Wentworth goes next Monday to the Bath for seven months with her two children. Lady Massam has not been with any body or received any visits at home this six weeks, and some says the Queen has ordered her to live very privately that she may not get the envy of the People, like the Duchess of Marlborough.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, July 18, 1712.

All the news I know is the Duke of Beaufort is so ill Dr. Ratlife says he can't live a month, though he goes a broad; but the Dr. says his longs are touched ocationed by former drinking. I beg of you for my sake as well as your own that you wont drink, for though you don't presently find the effects of it you see by the Duke of Beaufort what ill consequences comes after it. Perhaps you will think me very impertinent to pretend to advice you, but never the less when I think your health concerned I cant forbore Lord Rivers has writ to several of his friends from the Bath that he is much better than when he went down. Here is four named for Garters, Lord Treasurer, Duke of Kent, your self, and Lord Pawlet. I find non of the Court cares for Lord Pawlet.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: August 8, 1712.

I have found out a husband for Betty. He that is now Lord Winchelsy is old, so is his Wife, and no children; and my Lady Winchelsy has a son that will be Earl, which dus not dislike Betty nor she him, they yous to meet at Niece Hanbury's, I have seen him often, he is a pretty genteel welbred modest young man and sings fynly; his mother is a very subtle creature as lives, or else it might be easily dun. Could wee not get a place for him that would make up her little fortune, or have you no Dutchman for her, or was she made of honour her pretty face, fine shape, and three thousand pound added to what she has would get her of in a quarter of a year. Dear, dear soul pardon this long scroll from yrs &c.

note.value: WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: August 12, 1712.

I can never say half enough to your Lordship for your kindness in writing to me such a letter as I received last post, tired as you were with writing. I was almost in the spleen for want of hearing from you, but now I am refresh't with such a mark of your kindness, and the agreeable account of your progress to and from the army. I hope you are almost at the end of your trouble, and near coming home to enjoy the good place designed you, and the bleu ribbon, which I shall be overjoyed to see you adorned with. I never yet saw an instalment, but am resolved when yours is, to be one of your guests. I heard one piece of news lately that you can best tell the truth of, that Sir Henry Johnson is to be one of the Admiralty as well as yourself. I was again at Windsor last Sunday, and think the Queen looks and walks better then I have seen her in some years. Her subjects have for the most part been sick with a feavorish distemper that torments them extremely for some days. I have escaped it hitherto, but all else in the house have had it. Lord Rivers is languishing at the Bath without hopes of recovery, and will be succeeded in his title by a priest, but his estate will go as he pleases. Lord Scarsdale I find is going to Vienna, and Lord Bolingbrook expected back in a little time, and then they say we shall hear more of the Peace. If the french man you saw at Utrecht is poor, I believe him very honest, for he never asked me for any thing, and I have offered to lend him
money, if he had occasion, but his answer was that he wanted for nothing, tho I am apt to think his circumstances are not plentiful.

Your Lordship will wonder to hear I have sold Cane Wood. A Lord Blantire of Scotland offered me 4,000 pounds for it, which I thought worth hearkening to, considering the little time I stay out of town, and that a place of half that sum might serve me. I wish I may get a house in your neighbourhood of Twitnam, for I was always fond of that part of the country. I am still at Cane Wood, but would be glad to remove since it is none of my own. It seems it is the D. of Argyle hath bought it under another name, and I am desired to stay till the goods are valued, part of which he desires to buy. I forgot to tell you that soon after you went, I met Lord Treasurer who with a shake by the hand, told me that our friend My Lord Strafford was got well into Holland. I was not sorry to find that he knew I had the happiness of such a friend. The new Duke of Leeds is enraged at his father's will, who hath leapt over him to leave his estate to his son, and he threatens to pull him out of his coach. I could not but be sorry for the success the French have lately had, but am not at all so for the Dutch being humbled who seemed for some years to have lost the tramontane, and to forget what they and their neighbours were. I hope we shall soon be happy in a peace and no circumstance in it will please me more then the honour you are like to gain by it.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, November 25, 1712.

My brother Arundell has got the small-pox, and Mr. St. Amand thinks he cant live, which makes me defer making my men's surtout coats tell I see whethere he lives or dy's; for, for a brother's morning all people put there servants
in gray, and what won dos in that kind to doe like other people is in respect to won's self more than those won morns for. The Queen coms to town the latter end of the next week. I heard last night that the D. of Shrewsbery was declared for going to France, and that the Chancellor of the Exchecker is to have Mr. Manering's place preferring that before his own, being for life; and it is said Mr. Hambden is to turn tory and be made Chancellor of the Exchecer. Non of our lottry tickets are yet com up Prizes, what blanks I cant tell, for Mr. Ellison is not yet com to town.

TEI.text:
St. James's Square, December 16, 1712. I received the half pound of Bohea tea and it is extremely good. Here cam yesterday to me a warrant for a fat doe out of Windsor Park; I believe it is your fee upon being in the Admiralty, for it came from that office. They say the instalment will not be yet. I think I ought not to have writ so long a letter to you to day, for I am sure you'll have a very long won from Lady Wentworth with very great lamentation; for her monkey is dead. I have been as little merry as I could sense, for Lady W- was so much troubled about it that she was really angry if I laughed, and
you may believe it could be no affliction to me to make me melancholy, and I could not cry for my life. The day it died I expected Lady W- to diner and she nethere cam nor sent word, and I stayed diner for her some time, but she would not so much as see me that day. But what is the most extrodinary thing is she has two of its Pickturs drawn since it is dead, won large and the other in minatur. Now if Capt. Powell would ever oblige Lady W- he should make a copy of verses upon Pugg's death. Lord Treasurer's daughter was marred yesterday to Lord Carmarthan. It is said the Queen will make the Duchess of Hambleton a lady of the bedchamber to help to pay the debts. The Spanish Ambassador that is com over is the strangest dirty creature. I see him play at Beset with the Queen, and his hands were the dirtiest things I ever see.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, December 19, 1712.

I cant tell what you find it in Holland, but I think it the coldest winter I ever felt, though in all the snow the Queen goes out every day to take the air. The day for the instalment is not yet fixed; as soon as it is I'll let you know. It is now publicly talked that Lord Peterborough is to have Lord Rivers' regiment. The Queen has given Lord Carmarthen Mr. Dunce's lodgings in Whithall. Lord Treasurer went himself and fetched the Duke of Leeds to his son's wedding, and they say he behaved himself that day as well and with as much respect and kindness as any body could doe. Lord and Lady Pawlet was at the wedding, and she was in all her fine true lovers knots of diamonds set in as much silver as would make a pare of candlesticks. Non of your tickets is yet com up, except they are blanks; I have two 20 l. com up, but they will sell but for 15 l. a piece.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, December 23, 1712.

I cant help telling my Dearest Life that I never wished my self so much in Holland as now, for though you tell me it is only the tooth ack, others hear say you are ill. You may easly believe what a concern it is to me, I beg you for God's sake to take care of your self. Lady Wentworth has not been here this five days nor out of her chamber, and she still sent me word she was ill, but I fear she has heard you are ill and is in to great trouble to see me; for I have desired to wait on her every day and she never would give me leave but once. I never was so impatient for a post coming in as now. Last week it was reported here that you and Count Zinzendorf had fought a duel, sword and pistol, and that you ware killed, but they ware so good to me as to keep that from me tell they were convinced it was a lie. I wish I could be as well satisfied your illness is no more than what you say yourself. Here is a great many rumours talked of, as - the Duke of Beaufort to be Master of the horse and Lord Carmarthan to have his place, you to have the Ordnance, and the Duke of Leeds your place. Lord Fitzharding is dead who had two very good places, teller of the Exchecker and Treasurer of the Chamber. The teller's place I am told Lord Jersey expects, which is 2,000 l. a year; and Treasurer to the Chamber Lord De la War solicits for, and to quite his pension of 1,200 l. a year for it, they say that is 1.400 l. a year. Lord Portmore is to have the Duke of Hambleton's green Garter. I received this day 1 pound of tea directed to our Lady Wentworth, one to sister Betty, and 1/2 a pound to my self, which I have this moment tasted and it is extremely good. I conclude theirs is not so
good, but I'll keep that thought to my self. Lady Wentworth cam to town to night. I hope in God I shall have a letter from you to night with the joyful news of your being perfectly recovered. I own I was sorry for your having the tooth ask, but I cant say frighted, for though it was troublesome it was of no consequence; but the town says you are ill, which perfectly frets me out of my wits, for doe but consider what a miserable condition I must be in, whose whole happiness in this world intirly depends on your welfair, to hear you are ill. Adieu, pity won who truly loves you.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: December 26, 1712.

I was so pleased with your Lordship's kind remembrance of me in your letter that it made me insensible of any uneasiness
till I found you had been indisposed with a defluxion, a complaint that reigns much here, and which no body will escape, if this foggy weather continues, comparable to nothing but what I have heard is frequent at Amsterdam. I hope your Lordship is before this time perfectly recovered, and that I shall some way or other hear it soon. The news of the provinces coming into the Queen's measures is very agreeable here, and I hope every body thinks your share in that turn as great as I think you deserve. The battle in the north is also a great part of the conversation, and I own I had a secret pleasure in seeing Rosencrane's lofty looks a little humanised.

Otherwise I doe not know what is most desirable for us at this juncture. I dined last Sunday at the D. of Buckingham, who always loads me with civilities, and had a magnificent service of new guilt plate from the beginning of his dinner. He was full of this news, and seemed pleased. Lord Fitzharding is dead at last, and hath thought fit to leave me one of his executors, which will be no profit to me, but some trouble, having to doe with odd kind of people. However he hath left but few debts, and his two good places are very welcome to the ministry who have long had an eye upon them, but the Queen had the goodness to keep him in for his life. I had a visit that surprised me two days ago, of a young Spaniard, that came over with the ambassador. His name is Montejo, nephew to the famous Porto carrero. He had heard by a mistake that I had been to see him, which I was glad of, when I found him to have a great deal of wit, and a manner very engaging. Perhaps you may see him in Holland. He brought with him a Don Carlos de some thing, that I did not like so well. I was to look for them this morning but did not find them. I will endeavour to pick up some thing next time more worthy your attention.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, January 13, 1713.

In the first place I must tell my Dearest Life that I received your letter of the 17th a Sunday, and you bid me not be jealous of the woman that made those fine verses of you. I own to you I find your honour so very vain concerning your own person that there is no danger of your falling in love with anybody but your self; and pray tell Capt. Powell I say so, who I am sure will extremely agree with me in my opinion. I think it is really committing a sin to doe any thing to heighten your vainity, but at present I can't help it in telling you that everybody laments you are not to be instilled your self, because you would make so good a figure. The Duke of Kent told me a Sunday night that he and the rest of the Lords had agreed that the instalment shall be next Thursday seven-night, and that Lord Treasurer had given
money to the Wardrobe on purpose to pay for the Garter robes, &c., so I have sent Mr. Ellison to day to claim them, for I am told that is the custom; as to the Collar I can borrow won in case it should be wanting. Sir Jacob Banks was here this morning for he cam to town as soon as he had my brother's letter.

note.value: PASSAGE OMITTED
FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, January 13, 1713.

I received my dearest life's letter of the 18th this morning and thank you for that to Dr. Chamberlain. This letter will be a very dismal won to Capt. Powell since it brings the news of poor Lord Cornbery's death; he died yesterday morning of a fever got by a surfeit of drinking, for he and a good many more drank as many quarts of Uskquebath as is usall to be drank of wine, and was never cool after. Lady Theodotia will now be a great fortune, for Cobham is settled on her, and she is now Baroness of Cliffton. I have got your Garter robes from the Great Wardrobe, but I don't hear any time set for the instalment. I was a Tusday at Sir Godfry Kneller's, and there's the Duke of Buckingham drawn in his Garter robes, and I found out that Mr. De Gar has left out the Cross and Garter on the outward mantle, so I went to him and showed him where he had omitted it and ordered him to put it in.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St James's Square, January 27, 1713.

I have not heard from my Dearest life sense I write last. The only thing that is now talked of hear is of the French ambassador's house which was yesterday burnt down to the ground, and a house on each side of it. It was ocation'd from the confectioner's room which was at the top of the house, and the sugar's boiling over set fire of the bords and so of a great wooden beam. The whole street had been burnt if the Duke of Ormond had not by his great care prevented it. I had almost forgot to tell you that now I'll be vain in my turn, for a Sunday I was at court to inquire how the Queen did, and the French ambassador and several other foreigners said I was the handsomest woman there. You have so often told me of your beauty that I was resolved to return it as soon as I had any opportunity. The Whigg book I sent you by the last messenger was write by the Bishop of Salsbery's son.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: February 10, 1713.

I find I cannot hold, but must be scribbling some times whether I have anything to say or no. The finery of the
birth day's is not worth the troubling you with, and without a parliament this town doth not afford much. When that is to sit is yet a dispute, though appointed for next tuesday. The gentlemen grumble at their being kept so long to no purpose and I doe not know what humour they will be in when they doe meet. I must not forget one thing at the birth day, that My Lord Somers was there and hardly any other of his party. Your acquaintance Lord Cornbury had made fine clothes for that day, but was taken very ill with a fever that hath not yet left him. I was very sorry to hear of your pictures being stopped at the custom house, but hope you will get them off without paying 70 per cent. for your own goods, as if you were a merchant. I had the honour to play at Ombre lately with My Lady Strafford and Lady Portland. One hears no more of the instalment, then if there was to be none, and some think it will not be in so long time that you may be here your self, and not want a representative.
Lord Selkirk is gone or going very soon to France to solicit the pretensions of his family, which many say is nothing at all, and if anything My Lord Abercorne hath the right.

Notwithstanding the story I sent you word of hath been disproved to a degree very uncommon, yet many will not be persuaded out of it, and others affect to believe it. I have some remorse for not having writ to Capt. Powell, but he will have reason to thank me for escaping so dull a letter as must come at present.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, February 16, 1713.

I am told Lord Petterboroug is not at all pleased with Lord Treasurer's usage to him. A Saturday Lady Portland sent to me to desire I would com and spend the evening with her, and Lord Bartley was there, so we played at Ombra, and I can asure you his formality is in the greatest perfection at that game that ever I see it, and he has found out that I play extremely well at it which is what no body
ever found before. Mr. Harison was very fine on the Queen's birthday. If you had given Sir Jacob Banks ten thousand pound it would not have made him half so happy as being your proxy. The robes are all ready to be given out at the Wardrobe, and I hope to get yours to morrow. Sir Jacob Banks told my brother as Mr. Elleson was not in town he'd pay the fees for the robes, but I thought that would not look well to have him out of pocket, so I sent word that I would send him the money whatever it was, for I can asure you I can never employ any money I have so much to my own satisfaction as in pleasing you who I love much better than my self. Adieu!

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, February 17, 1713.

In the first place my Dear I received your letter of the 22nd a Saturday by Lord Privy Seal's gentleman who very civilly came to me and brought me the lace clouts and tea as soon as he cam; and brought me a fine compliment from good Mrs. Robinson and Lord Privy Seal, and as he brought me the things safe I gave him a ginney. Mr. Harrison died last Saturday and is very much lamented by all that knew him here. His brother Poets buried him, as Mr. Addison, Mr. Philips, and Dr. Swift. I can tell you the reason the Duchess of Rutland did not go to court on the Birthday; the Duke is so great a Whigg that he did not care she should go. I can asure you I was set out in very great order for the Spanish Ambassador and he said I had won of the best houses he had been in. There was a Spanish Duke and another noble man of Spain that cam over with them; Mons. Forcerner brought them, and my brother was here with me. I can tell you there is 3 people already named for Mr. Harrison's place, Mr. St. John's (Lord Bullingbrock's
brother), Mr. Hare, and Mr. Watkins that had the place before. The Queen is still confined to her dressing room. I am really told the Queen is mightily concerned for Lord Cornbery, and sent herself twice a day to know how he did; he was jest agoing to have had Lord Windsor's regiment. I have again played at Ombra with Lord Barkley, and he has now found that nobody plays better than I. If you are ever jealous of anybody it must be Lord Barkley, for I have heard in several places where he has said no man in the world was so happy in a wife as you. You know I am like you and have no vanity at all, so to be sure I don't believe what he says.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, March 3, 1713.
Dear Brother,

Although last Saturday Lord T- shook several country gentlemen, members of the house of Commons, by the hand,
and told them that the night before there was a courier arrived from France and that all was agreed to - the King of France having left all matters in dispute to the Queen and that now the house would set to do business.

How the Whigs came to know it the Lord know; but they laid wagers that the Queen would not go this day to the house and that the house would not set to do business, so that all the hearty Tories that my Lord T- did the favour to speak to have lost their money, and are laughed at into the bargain. They begin now to murmur much and not to understand the jest of such bites.

The Queen was abroad in her chair Friday and Saturday, and she looked very well, and I hope to God she's so. It was in order to use herself to the air to be able to go to the house to day as was given out, but since she did not go that banter has been much censurer .

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, March 24, 1713.

The child was christened last Saturday. The Queen sent Lady Katthern Hyde (as being the Lady in waiting) and the Duchess of Kent stood for Lady Wentworth, and Lord Treasurer was here. I believe the Queen considers my vainity and designs to make you a Marquise, for the custom is when she stands godmother to a Lord, she sends 20 ginneys to the nurses, to an Earl, 30, and to a Marquis, 40, and she sent 40 here. I began to see company a Sunday, and am to sit in order tell Thursday; all the Queen's ladies has been here and every body admires our house. Mr. Shales has been very civil in lending me a great deal of plate. I think the bed the handsomest made up I have seen any where, and a great many is gon away with the thoughts that the gilt leather is gold brocaded stuff. Lady Essex was yesterday to see me; she never visited me before, she cam to desire me to give you a great many thanks for your civilities to her son and says she believes he is so fond of being at your house that she feared he was very troublesome. The French ambassador now begins to be very entertaining to the Ladies, for every Thursday he makes a very fine super, and has muskick and asks some Lady of quality to com and invite her own company.
Last Thursday the Duchess of Richmond was Lady of it, and this Thursday the Duchess of Buckingham is to be.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: I am always infinitely obliged to your Lordship for allowing me a place in your thoughts when crowded with so many great affairs, and showing a concern for anything that happens to me, particularly in this executourship of My Lady Bellasis, which proves very considerable, and was so little expected that it is in a manner fallen from the clouds. I return thanks at the same time for the little book, which is valuable in its kind, and hath a recommendation to me in having your name in it, that I am always glad to

You will see by the speech which the Queen made yesterday, for which the commons ordered thanks immediately, but the Lords would not let it go without a debate, and were beat by a majority of two and thirty, there were long speeches that amounted to no more I think then that it did not become their prudence to give thanks for anything before they knew what it was.

My Lord Halifax was the first opposer, then My Lord Cooper, Lord Sunderland Lord Nottingham and his brother. Lord Treasurer said that an address of thanks did not preclude any enquiry into the peace and there would be an examination into the endeavours used these two years to obstruct so good a work. Lord Peterborough said it was known by every body that there had been an endeavour to make a captain general for life. My Lord Sunderland took it up, saying it was a thing of great consequence if true,
therefore he would doe well to prove it. The other answered nothing.

I was sorry I could not be at Council last Tuesday, where the articles of peace were read and ratified. My Lord Cholmley is since that turned out, and so is Sir Richard Temple. To morrow at two oclock is appointed to present the address.

note.value: FROM LADY ISABELLA WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p:
What would I give to see Stattyra and Roxseany together. My neic Pie and her husband and children goes to day to Twitnam, they have taken a house thear, and so my nephew Peeter Batthurst has dun. Did I ever tel you the church is fallen down, and the fat minister is dead and Doctor Pratt, he that taught the Duke of Gloster, is minister? So before it fell he preached one sermon in it, but would
preach no more, but ordered Pasmore to make a tabernakle in the church yard, which al has and must contribute to.
