So he preached thear and exhorted al to give thancks for thear great deliverance for the church not falling when they wear in it, it being then standing. The people all laughed at him, and in a week's time it fell down to the ground, so all the parish contrebutse to the building of it. I hear Sir Jams Ash has given a hundred pt, his daughter that is but fourteen has given three scour, his blind sister a hundred, Mrs. Windom fifty, Lady Tufton fifty, and her son fifty, Lady Humble fifty, Mr. Boucher forty. This I harde by a Twitnam body att Whithall church.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p:
I cannot forbear writing some times to put you in mind of your humble servant and old acquaintance, though my head is so full of the business of trade, with hearing of nothing else, within and without the house of Lords, that it puts out all other thoughts, and yet I know so little of it that I should get no credit with speaking of it. There hath been high feuds in the house of commons, for after all the time spent, and debates past, it hath been the opinion of many, that it was best to let it drop. None were so warm for this opinion as My Lord Anglesey, and Sir Thomas Hanmer. The Whigs are apparently elevated at this division, who must have this justice done them that they observe better discipline, but the others all think themselves fit to govern. There hath been a quarrel between the D. of Bucks and Lord Conway about a law suit in which his Grace was cast, who said that he declared before God that notwithstanding he lost it, he had done nothing but what was justifiable, and if My Lord Conway had been his son he could not have done more. This one would think carried no provocation in it, but My Lord Conway answered that he would rather be any man's son in England then his, and the D. of Be replied that he would
rather have anybody for his son then such a fool as he. This occasioned a challenge, but mischief was prevented. Your Lordship hath heard of My Lord Dorset's being out of Warden of the cinq ports. I wondered less at his going out then his staying in so long when he opposed the court in every thing, but it seems he assured several people that he would be for the malt bill, though he had been for breaking the Union, but when it came to the question, voted against it. I believe there are not many people concerned for him. The house of Commons sat last night till eleven a clock, and flung out the trade bill by 9 only. It makes a sad breach among the Ministers and their friends, and occasions much grumbling and complaints. It is a dispute beyond me, and I will say nothing to it, nor trouble you any longer.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Richmond, August 4, 1713.

I am extremely peevish at myself for troubling your Lordship with a tedious account of Blenheim, quite forgetting that you had seen it which now I perfectly remember. I will not repeat the same fault about your own house at Twitnam where I past an hour very pleasantly last week, but I cannot help saying that I find it so much improved that I can hardly think it is the same place, and I think it altogether extremely pretty. I am in a very ugly house at Richmond, but like the airings about it very much. I was uneasy at first with thinking that one could never be alone in a town so full of company, but find one is seldom hurt by the things one is afraid of. I am sorry your Lordship hath had so ill success about the chaplain, and wish I may be more lucky to him, but in almost three years I have not been able to provide for a very deserving clergy man, a kinsman of my wife's. Men of that function are very long lived. I have often been told of several being given over that are yet alive. There are about five and forty livings in the Duchy. The greatest number small ones, but seven or eight very good ones. The best that hath fallen in my time was one in Lincolnshire worth not above one hundred pounds a year, in the fenny part where few people care to go. Perhaps after such a long time a good many
may go off together. I would promise your Lordship the first that falls, if I was not engaged to the gentleman I mentioned. There is also one in Hertfordshire that I have promised, but after that I am free, and your Lordship may command me, for I will never promise any other. If one of a hundred pounds a year would content Mr. Ayerst, perhaps I might be able to serve him sooner, till a better falls. However he may depend upon what I can doe, after that gentleman is provided for, and I shall be impatient to have it in my power to doe a thing you so much desire. I am entirely of your mind about Benson. Every year that house receives some great blow, that I am persuaded (setting aside my being a member of it), it is the interest of the public to have its dignity kept up. Your servants at Twitnam told me they expected you in a fortnight, but by your saying nothing of it, I conclude it is a mistake.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, March 5, 1714.
Dear Brother,

The first thing the lords did after thanking the queen for her speech was to condemn a Pamphleet called the Spirit
of the Whigs in answer to the Crisis. Lord Wharton made the motion seconded by the Duke of Devonshire, but Lord W- was out in his intended introduction of the matter, for he begun by telling the house, as he past through the court of request this Book was put into his hand and lighting accidentally upon the 20th and 21st page were the reflection upon the whole Scotch Nation is; but when he came to read the words he had bought a second edition, were those pages were left out, so he was forced to call to some lords that had the first edition in their pockets. I have the first Edition which I'll send you by the first Messenger that goes, it is writ with a great deal of spirit, the Whigs guesses it to be Dr. Swift's. The lords have the Printer in costody, who they say will not confess, but if the worst comes to the worst, I hear they have found out a man that will own, which will save the Doctor's Bacon. Mr. Gore has not acquitted himself very well of the part that was assigned him in the house of Commons. As soon as the Speaker had returned to the house with the Queen's Speech and had read it to the house, Mr. Gore rise up with a paper in his hat which he did not read well, to make the motion of thanks, and repeated the Queen's speech word for word, so that Sir Joseph Jekell observed upon him that the spirit of prophecy was not ceased, for there was a gentleman that know the Queen's speech before she spoke it, for it was impossible to remember it upon the first reading; but however the question that was concerted went cleverly, and the Commons are come into a warmer address then the Lords. I don't know the reason but stock still does not rise. The next book that the Lords fall upon will be that of the Hereditary Right; the commons when they have time to consider Pamphleets will begin with the Crisis and English &c. I have sent you a Ballet, because I heard of the accident when I was with you at Dover, and the last four lines are very much sung by the Whig Ladies. I have no news to send you but that I thank God the Queen continues well and after chapel to-day touch a great many poor people.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p:
I have forbore till now troubling your Lordship with my letters, conscious of my inability either to inform or divert you, but after the favour you have expressed to me in so kind and so long a letter, it is impossible to be silent. I could not have believed your Lordship so much master of french, as I see you are. It is so long since I writ in that language, that I am sure I could not approach you in choice of words, and clearness of expression I did hear something of a Servant of yours running distracted, but not of his being a Spy. I am glad Bothmar had the mortification you gave him about it. I am much pleased with what the Electric says to you of her having the names of Whigs and tories, invented only by ill designing people, but ought to be detested by all honest men, as well as by Princes, who should be above listing themselves in any. It is spoke like a great Princess. Notwithstanding the aspersions that have been thrown there is such an aversion to popery, that I believe in my conscience, the generality thinks of nothing after the Queen, but the house of Hanover. As for Scotland I doubt the case is a little different. The house of Lords hath been taken up with a book called the public Spirit of the Whigs, where the Scotch are most unsufferably abused, but doe not show half the resentment that other people show. Much bustle hath been made to find the Author to no purpose It is imagined to be Swift, who hath more wit then judgment. They say this will occasion an examination of other pamphlets who are so bold as to attack the Queen and her ministers. It would be happy if it would occasion some restraint of the intolerable liberty of the press. The Commons were on Saturday upon Mr. Steel who hath been very
free in his writings, but he hath had time allowed him till Thursday next. They talk much of the D. of Argyle's loosing his places, and My Lord Stair's, who hath played and lived at such a rate that he will be quite undone if he is turned out. To return again to Mr. Steel he makes a sad bustle still about Dunkirk, and moved yesterday that an address might be presented for all papers relating to that place to be laid before the house, but he and his friends were beat by a great majority. Here are people that will face you down that there is not one bit of the fortifications of Dunkirk demolished. For my part I cannot but be sorry that they are, since I am persuaded it might be of great use by its nearness to the Downs where we have always ships, and should be pleased to have some of our ancient footing on the continent. I am apt to think both the French and Dutch are glad to have it demolished. Upon My Lord Cooper's motion, to morrow is appointed to go upon the Q.'s speech, when I suppose all the venom will be port out. Her Majesty had last week a little fit of an ague, but is very well again.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: April 6, 1714.
My Lord,

I should have troubled your Lordship with a letter before this time if any thing material had fallen within my knowledge; I'm sure your Lordship must have had an account of Mr. Steele's affair in the House of Commons, which is the only bustle that has been there yet.

The House of Lords have been calling for several papers and last friday entered upon some of them. They read a Narrative which was laid before them, in which was contained an account of the whole progress of the Peace and what was wanting to make it Universal, and what obstructions her Ma~ty had met with during the Negotiation. This was laid before them in pursuance of an Address they had made. My Lord Cooper and My Lord Halifax debated only of the
part which related to the Catalans, they confessed they were glad to find that so much had been done and such endeavours had been used to obtain their ancient privileges for them, and they concluded with a Motion for an Address that the Queen would continue her most pressing endeavours that they might be restored to all their privileges. Lord Chancellor closed in with the Motion, making an addition att the beginning, viz., to thank her Ma~ty for what she had already done, and to express the satisfaction of the House in the Methods that had been used for obtaining those conditions for the Catalans. This putt an end to the Debate and Saturday they cooked up the Vote into an Address.

One thing seems a little in the Dark to me which I believe your Lordship can set in a true light - How it came to pass that the business of the Catalans was given up on a sudden, when it had been propped so earnestly all along.

I began this yesterday morning, and must now fill up the rest with what happened in the Debate yesterday. I have endeavoured to get the best account I could from Lords of my acquaintance, for no body was suffered to hear the Debate who was not of the House except Baron Schutts, who staid in the whole day. Lord Wharton began a general attack upon the Peace, called it a bad bargain, a lamentable conclusion of such a glorious war, &c.; then he set forth the Dangers we were in from France and expatiated upon all the common topicks the Whiggs are daily talking in Coffee Houses. Lord Nottingham afterwards made another Harangue, and after him Lord Townshend, but they concluded without any Motion, only general complaints. Upon which Lord Bolingbrook took notice how difficult it was to make a reply to such discourses that aimed att no particular point, and wherein no Method was observed, but he thought what was said might be reduced under three Heads, objections to the Peace in general, the manner of making it, and the non execution of some parts of it. He spoke to every one of these Heads, and answered what was alleged by every Lord who had spoke before him. The Arguments on both sides cant be brought within the Compass of a letter neither would
these be any thing new to your Lordship. I shall only mention two points that were insisted on to prove the Non-execution of the treaty, that Dunkirk was not demolished, and that Placentia was not in our Hands. Your Lordship can judge how easily those points could be answered. My Lord Bolingbrook concluded with the matter relating to the removal of the Pretender from Lorraine, in which he set forth what had been already done, and that he was ready to agree to any thing that could be further proposed, but hoped that groundless assertions would not be thrown upon those who had the Honour to serve her Ma~ty. After the Debate had held some time, without tending to any particular Point Lord Ferrers said he thought it was time to propose a question that they might come to some conclusion, so he moved that the Succession in the House of Hanover was not in danger. When Lord Chancellor read it he had added the words (under her Matys government); they said that was not the Question, for my Lord Ferrers had moved it without those words, but My Lord said he want it so. They said that as to her Maty no body could have a thought that it was in any danger from her, but for her Ministers that was another case.

Lord Anglesey opposed it violently and fell a railing against all the proceedings of the Peace, he said he had been one of those who was for indicating the Suspension of Arms, not for any reasons he had heard within doors but for some he was told without, viz. that there was a peace concluded advantageous to this Nation and secure to all the Allies, that the Protestant succession was effectually secured by it, and that we should have such a trade as would bring in 2 millions per annum ; What there was of all this that proved true their Lordships could now judge. He said a good deal more with a great deal of Warmth and concluded that if the Succession was not in danger before, this Vote would make it so.

They divided att last upon the additional words and it was carried that those words (under her Matys government) should be added. Contents 66, Prox. 11; Non. 53, Prox. 10. Lord Windsor has left his Prox. with Lord Orrery who was not content. It was near 9 when this was over, and then the
Duke of Bolton renewed a motion which he had made just after Lord Ferrers made his, for an Address to the Queen to give a reward to any one who should take the Pretender dead or alive if he landed in Britain or Ireland. That was agreed to without opposition. Another motion was made by Lord Halifax which was joined to the former, that the Queen should be desired to get the Emperor and all those Princes who had been in Alliance with her to be guarantees for the Protestant Succession. This was not opposed neither, they are to putt this Vote into an address and letter to be brought before the House on thursday, and then it is said that other matters are also to be debated.

If your Lordship will pardon the Defects of this account I shall endeavour to send you a further of what may occur remarkable in either House. I shall judge whether your Lordship will permit me to continue a Correspondent by the Answer you return, for if you send me no news from the Hague in return for this Bundle I send you, I shall take it for granted you would not be troubled with any more, but if you should be very busy and can't afford time for to send news, you may fill your letter with some of your D. Dossunas snuff for once.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, April 16, 1714.
Dear Brother,

They tell me Lord Be Narrative will be printed, or else before this I would have endeavoured to have sent it you. You'll see by the printed votes how the business went yesterday in the house of Commons; and to day I have been an eavesdropper at the door of the house of Lords and have staid so long to hear how matters went there that I can't this post tell you the particulars I have gathered; only that, the Question was carried for thanks to the Queen for the care she has taken of her subjects, notwithstanding the obstructions she has met with, and the desire of the lords that she'll continue with the same steadfastness to promote the general good of Europe. In short the Question was carried by 19.
The Bishop of London was with the Court now, and I believe Lord Angelsea was so to, for he did not speak a word in this day's debate.
The truth is I have been so long fasting that I am gone to eat and drink and defer writ more particular till next post.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My Lord,

Since I had the Honour to write last to your Lordship there have been several debates in the House of Lords which if I were able to give you a good account off, it would be a very great satisfaction to me, finding the last I sent was not unacceptable to your Lordship.

But my misfortune is that I never have time to write, though I have nothing else to do, and yet I do assure your Lordship if I really had a great deal of business upon my hands I should be ready to neglect any part of it rather than fail to obey your Lordship's commands, but being constantly engaged in some party or other every night, the greatest difficulty is to sit down to write. I have reserved this morning on purpose to try to recollect as much as I can what I have picked up of the last week's debates.

There was an address moved by the D. of Bolton about taking the Pretender, Dead or Alive; it was asked in the House whether if any Person should shoot him or poison him he would not be guilty of Murder. Lord Trevor gave his opinion that by the Law of England he certainly would, and upon that consideration it was agreed to turn it to give the reward to any one who should apprehend him and bring
him to justice in case he landed or attempted to land. Another alteration was made in the address by Lord North to leave it to the Queen when She saw convenient. The Answer (which I suppose you have seen already) took notice that She did not att present see any occasion for issuing out this Proclamation, but would do it when ever it was necessary and that the most effectual security to the Hanoverian Succession was to putt an end to groundless jealousies &c. Lord Wharton fell upon this next day and said he was afflicted to the last degree with this unkind answer to so dutiful an address. He knew her Majestys goodness was such that She would never take any thing in ill part from her House of Lords, unless some bold whisperer had misrepresented their debates and intentions, therefore the Ministry ought to answer for this, &c. The debate lasted some time in this manner, other Lords urging that the House had left it to her Majesty to take her own time in issuing the Proclamation, but the Whig-Lords insisted upon the latter part of the Answer in which they said the Queen charged that house with being the Authors of groundless jealousies. Upon that Lord Trevor explained the Queen's meaning to be that She approved of the pains the House had taken in considering of the state of the Nation and agreed with them that the proper and only means to secure the Succession was to putt an End to jealousies, as the House had endeavoured to do by the Vote they passed that the Succession was not in Danger. Upon this Lord Abingdon moved an address of thanks to her Majesty for Her gracious answer and that they would continue to doe their utmost to secure the Succession and to prevent those jealousies which had been so universally and industriously spread over the Nation.
I may mistake the exact words of these motions for I have not got any copies by me but I think I remember the sense right.
I must now tell you that the whiggs moved the words and not without reason and the tories added and industriously in the room of them, for the motion was made without either.

Another day the D. of Argile and Lord Townshend fell
upon the Treasurer for a sum of money which they found to be paid to some Highlanders in Scotland, who they said were Nonjurors and Papists and they moved that some persons who were now in town might be summoned to appear before the House to be examined about this matter. Lord Wharton said that the Ministers ought to give an account of this, they must not shelter themselves under the Queen's authority, for what ever the Queen did the Ministers that advised it were to answer for. Upon that Lord Treasurer spoke, and much bolder and clearer than ever I heard him before. He said he would always stand by that maxim, and should att any time be willing to be tried upon it, and he hoped that some rule would be observed whenever they came upon the consideration of matters passt under the last Ministry. As to the calling of witnesses he said there was no manner of occasion for it in this case, for he owned that he had paid this money, he owned that he had advised the giving it, and therefore hoped that they would immediately come to a censure if they thought he deserved it, for having effected that service for the sum of 3500 l. , for which in a former reign 16000 l. had been given without effect. In short Lord Townshend who made the Motion said he was satisfied and thought My Lord Treasurer had cleared the matter and desired it might be dropped. But then Lord Bolingbrook got up and said it would be very hard that after this matter had been brought upon the stage and an accusation had been framed against the noble Lord (who had done as great service to his Country and with the least gain to himself that ever any Minister had done), it should be dropped without doing him the justice to declare him innocent, when they own they thought him so. Upon that he moved a Question, that the said sum was well applied, and it passt without a division. This passage which I have last mentioned will in some measure give an answer to one part of your Lordship's letter, for you will find by this that those great men agree very well in public what ever little scuffles they may have in private. Your intelligence of an answer given in writing and a Lady's interposing to make up a
quarrel, is what I never heard, and I can venture to say has no foundation. I believe there has been some quarrels but the Queen her self interposed and keeps them together; how long things will continue in this posture I can't determine. But now I must go on to another day's work which was the greatest of all. The Peace was considered and the D. of Argile spoke with a great deal of warmth, showed what a Posture the Nation was in to have commanded any Peace, how weak the Enemy; he said he had since passt through their country and it was not to be expressed how miserable the People were, but by our cessation of Arms we had scandalously deserted our Allies, and made a shameful Peace, and so run down every article. I can't remember the exact words. There was a great deal said on both sides, but I should tire your patience quite out if I undertook to run through all that, for there was nothing could be said new upon that subject which has been so sifted for 2 years past. The Bishop of London spoke, but it was only in answer to the Bishop of Serum who endeavoured to persuade the Lords for conscience sake not to approve the Peace, which he said was founded upon perfidy, in that we had broke our treaties with our Allies. Att last the Question was carried that the Peace was safe, honourable, and advantageous, and to desire her Majesty to go on in such measures as would make the same complete. I shall lose the post if I add any more or stay to make a handsome conclusion.
It was carried by a Majority of 19.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My Lord,

Had any thing happened here since my last in the least worth your Lordship's notice I should not have failed to have done my self the Honour of sending it to you. I never was inquisitive after News before now, and always abhorred a long debate, but the hopes of having some thing to write to you (after you have been pleased so very obligingly to accept of my poor Correspondence) makes me long for an occasion that may furnish me with matter to give you some entertainment. Nothing has passt in the House of Lords but the hearing of Causes. One of them has made some noise because it seemed to be made a party matter. Rooper the Protestant heir of Rooper deceased (but a pretty distant relation) sued Constable and Ratcliff, 2 Papists, for a sum of money that was left to them, about 10,000 l. ; the point that it turned upon was this, that this money was to arise by a Sale of Lands and the Act of Parlt says no papist shall have any lands or profits out of lands by Purchase. The Lawyers explain the word Purchase to signify any way what soever that a man has a thing, that is not by descent, but not to trouble you with the particulars of a cause upon which the Judges (of whom 11 were present) spent 5 long hours in arguing, there happened to be 6 of them for reversing, and 5 for affirming the Decree. The Whiggs who were very zealous to show their abhorrence of Popery, attended to a man, the others, (of whom several were in doubt which way the Cause ought to go in justice, and several in prudence did not care to appear for Papists upon any account) made a very small number, and did endeavour to prevent a division. Your humble servant was one of those who remained in doubt and did not vote, but one thing must be taken Notice of, that as this Act of Parlt was explained by Lord Chief Justice Parker all the Marriage Settlements of the Papists are overturned, they can't be able to lend money upon a Mortgage, they can't recover any debt from any Man who has not a personal Estate, and most of those who are now in Possession
of Estates in Land have and ought to forfeit them to the next Protestant heir. What consequences may follow upon this I can't tell; but I think it is necessary the Act should be made perfectly clear and intelligible which att present it is not. It seems Jack How brought it in in K. William's time to endeavour to throw Popery att his Head, and by that means it past in a Hurry, and nothing has ever been tried upon it before the case I have mentioned.

Your Lordship may judge of the Dearth of news when I have been forced to fill a letter with the report of a Cause, but there is one thing I must give you an account of, though I don't know what ground there is for it. It is reported all about town to day that the D. of Cambridge is coming over immediately and they say that letters came in last night to some Whigg Lords with positive assurances of it. Your Lordship will know more of the truth of this matter on your side of the water and I beg you will let me know your opinion of it when you are next att leisure to give me a line.

I have not heard any thing of Lord Paget's going, though it was said att first that he would go in a few days. I don't doubt but your Lordship's intelligence will prove true, though I'm att a loss att present to account for your quick alteration. I know your Lordship must have had an account of the Queen's illness from better hands; I hope she will in a short time be perfectly recovered. I have now nothing more to add in relation to public affairs, and therefore beg leave now to congratulate you upon your hopes of a son which I doe assure you no body (not excepting my Aunt Wentworth her self) does more heartily wish for. My Wife was brought to bed of one last week, and I think, besides the satisfaction of having two strings to one's bow, it is so great a comfort that it is not a Daughter, that I have the utmost desire your Lordship may have the same success.

The Courier has not yet brougt me the Snuff, but I return your Lordship ten thousand thanks; and as to the other parcel, if your Lordship will send over a pound when you have an opportunity that will keep me a great while and I shall be extremely thankful.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My Lord,

Since I had the Honour to write last to your Lordship I received the snuff, which is very good, and I return your Lordship a thousand thanks. I could not omit writing upon that account, but besides that, I know if I mist another post, you would interpret it to proceed from negligence, and not from want of news, though I beg that you will be assured I shall never fail in keeping up the Correspondence you Honour me with, unless I am entirely unprovided with any thing worth the reading. Now that is a good deal my Case att this time. The 2 Houses have been adjourned during the Holidays, and they are the main Springs from whence all the News on this side flows. To tell you who was hanged, who married, who died of small-pox or feavours looks more like a Bill of mortality than a letter. But for want of other matter I'll send you Something of that. Poor Mr. Pooley (who was somewhere abroad some time ago) hanged himself last week, he has been sick and melancholy a good while, and has had his head much perplexed about religion. I think there are not many here who are in danger from that quarter, but there is a bill brought in this day into the House of Commons to prevent the growth of schism, which if it takes effect may in time prevent the Mischiefs that are likely to arise from false pretentions to religion. It is chiefly to hinder Seminaries of Non-con. Ministers. I have not seen it yet, and therefore can give but an imperfect account.

People talk still of Divisions att Court, what ground there is for that I can't tell. These last 2 days the Discourse has been that Lord Bolin-k would be turned out, but if I can guess any thing he stands as firm as any One whatsoever. His Parts make him generally esteemed, and his other good qualities as generally beloved. Time only will show us what is the truth of these matters. In the mean time I can only send the idle rumours of the town. I wish your Lordship all prosperity and am ever yours.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My Lord,

I have received your Lordship's present of snuff by Mr. Bromley, it is extremely good and there is enough to last me a great while. I have sent your Lordship the Paper which was laid before the House of Commons, you can't oblige me more than in laying any commands upon me, but your Lordship will find this is only a part, and called for by the House upon a particular account which was the paying of the foreign troops. There was a debate the other day in the House of Commons whether the Hanover troops should be paid till the time of the Cessation of Arms; it was argued on one side that her Maty had given them notice that if they did not obey the commands of her General she would not pay them, and therefore it was not usual for the House to give money when it was not demanded by the Crown; on the other side the Justice of the matter was urged that they should have their pay for the time they did serve, that they were hired to carry on a war against France, and that it was contrary to the Grand Alliance to come to such a Cessation of Arms without the Consent of all the Allies; that it might be reckoned to be demanded by the Crown as well as any other money because it came before the House in as regular a manner as any other, that it had come from the Treasury, &c. but att last upon a division it was carried by a great Majority for the leaving of the Chair; so the matter remains unsettled and to be resumed whenever the House thinks fit.

I have no other News to send your Lordship but the melancholy account of the Duke of Beaufort's death, who was just got into the Country, and after having heated himself a shooting in the morning he drunk a great quantity of small Liquor which made him vomit Blood and he died in three days after.

This is so small a Packet that I did not think it necessary to send it about but I shall observe your Lordship's directions
when there is occasion, and only beg that your Lordship would take as many opportunities as you can to lay any of your commands upon &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My Lord,

I acquainted your Lordship in my last what a sad Dearth of News and Politics we laboured under, and I was in great hopes that this bill of Scism would have occasioned some Debate that might have furnished me with matter for your Entertainment. It was for that reason I deferred writing
you last post expecting the Grand Debate would have been this day, but unluckily tic putt of till wednesday; then the Bill is to be committed and that will be the Day of Battle.

I don't doubt but this matter will very soon (if it is not already) be talked off in Holland, and I take it for granted it will be represented there as the beginning of a Persecution. I will therefore state to your Lordship as well as I can what the design and tenor of this Bill is. There was an Act of Uniformity past in Queen Elizabeth's time, another in Charles the 2d, which are printed in all our common prayer Books that they might be the more publicly observed. However in direct defiance of these laws the Dissenters have been very industrious in setting up Schools and Seminaries and have gone upon a Notion that the Toleration has set aside those laws. Now this Bill is only to give a new life to those old Laws, and to take care that these troublesome People (who generally differ from the Established constitution in State matters as much as in Church) may not increase, and by brooding up their children in the same way perpetuate those unhappy divisions we have amongst us. I know that in Holland they take no such method, but they observe one rule which effectually secures them, and makes all other precaution needless, which is that nobody has a right to Vote upon any occasion who is not of the Established religion. Thus I am informed it is with them. I wish it were so here and after that I should think there could be no manner of Danger from these Dissenters, and for my own part I should be for ever after entirely disposed to favour them in any thing they desired.

Thus much of my letter my Lord I wrote this day senight and happened to miss the post that night and therefore kept it with a design to finish it the next. We had that day again a very long day about the same bill, and I dined afterwards in company and did not come home in time to finish it or send it. Since we have had nothing to doe or talk off but this bill ever since, I thought I could not do better than to send your Lordship the same which I had begun upon the subject, that I might att the same time give your Lordship
some proof that it has been by misfortune and not negligence that I have been so long without putting your Lordship in mind of me. This day the bill was read the third time and past, carried by a majority of eight only. They have made several alterations but in substance it is still the same as it was sent up from the Commons, only a clause is now added which makes it take effect in Ireland as well as England. Yesterday the Lord L-t of Ireland came into the House and spoke against its being extended to Ireland, the reasons he gave were because they had no act of Toleration there and that the Act of Uniformity was putt in Execution, and that as long as he had any thing to do there it should be putt in Execution; therefore he thought it needless, and besides to take a whole Kingdom in by a clause he thought not so proper as to bring in a Bill for that purpose. My Lord Chancellor answered him and took notice that his Lordship thought that putting the Act of Uniformity in Execution in Ireland would do no manner of Harm, which was a great satisfaction to him to hear from a Noble Lord who was just come from there, and gave a full answer to all the Objections that were raised in the last day's debate by Lord Wharton and others who threatened dismal consequences from it. As to the Objection that it was not proper or necessary nor decent to do it by a clause, he thought nothing could so properly be done by a clause in relation to that Kingdom (as a great many Instances could be given of things that had been done in that matter) as this, which was only to invigorate an act that they already had and that was thought to be a good one, and which upon Experience they had found to be so; this was chiefly intended to make the prosecution more easy and to remove an evil which every body acknowledged to be one and some thought a very growing one. Upon that his Grace got up and desired to explain himself as to one matter, he said he did not allege that there had been any one brought to punishment upon that Act in his time; but that there had been a prosecution began and that the person had submitted, and so the prosecution was stopped. Lord Anglesey then got up and said he had known Ireland some time, but he never
knew any prosecution of that nature take effect; he knew of a person who was prosecuted for building a meeting-house, but upon his submission and promise to leave it off the prosecution was stopped, and as soon as the prosecution was stopped he went on again. It was built, and had been preached in ever since in open defiance of the law.

The question was then putt and every body continued in the same mind they were off before. I believe I could recollect some other passages in the long transactions of this bill, but I'm afraid I have tired your Lordship already, and I'm going to night out of town, and it is already dark.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, August 3, 1714.
Dear Brother,

Before this you will know we have lost our good Mistress. I am sensible I should have felt her goodness more, if it had not been for a wicked one about her, God forgive; her I forgive, and I fear those whose interest it was the most to have kept her alive hasten her Death; for Doctor Shadwell tells me and all the world that when he felt her Pulse a Wednesday before dinner he did not like it and asked her how she did, she say very well, he said he should be glad she was, but by her pulse he was sure she was not, and went from her and told it to the Duke of Shrewsbury who went to see her, but she was busy so did not, but sent Dr. Alburtenhead who after Dinner brought the Duke word her Pulse was well, and the same thing he made Dr. Slown say, for they had always had a mind to keep the Queen's illness a secret. The town tell a world of stories of Lady Masham now; as that a Friday she left the Queen for three hours to go and ransak for things at St. James's. I can't say if this is true or false, a saturday I remember particularly I see her go away, but as I thought with too much grief, to have any thoughts of herself. I hope people wrong her, for she would be a monster in nature to be ungrateful and to forget a Queen so soon that raised her from nothing.

Lord Bullingbrook sunday made a Bonfire and the finest
illumination in town at his house in Golden Square, but that might be out of Policy fearing the mob, but there was no occasion for this precaution, for King George was proclaimed very Peaceably and ever thing has continued ever since.

I was in hopes you would come over upon this ill news, and after having taken care of your self made interest for me that I might be a groom of his Bedchamber, for I would not be a Equerry all my life time. That's an employment that none can lay claim to but the late King's Bedchamber, and here's some of them dead; but if you can't succeed for me in that I hope you will endeavour to get me some Patent Place, or a Commissioner of the Custom house or Excise.

It is said there are schemes sent over to the King already, and they that are upon the spot with him will have an addvantage, which I hope may be your case whatever becomes of your poor unfortunate brother.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: August 10, 1714.
My Lord,

I believe your Lordship will think I might have had sufficient matter to fill a letter during this month, and therefore will accuse me of Negligence if I don't give some account of my self. I must therefore begin with telling you that I went into Gloucestershire about business the very day the Parliament rose and came back to town but a few days before the Poor Queen fell ill. I was going out of town again that very day when I heard she was taken with a fit (as they called it) of an Apoplexy. I went immediately to Kensington and found there was no room to expect her life. She did indeed hold out beyond every body's expectation. Every thing has been so quiet since her death, and we go on so unanimously in both Houses of Parliament for his Majesty's service that I have nothing of any moment to mention upon that head, only that the Tories in the House of Commons are the Persons that appear most forward to do the King's business. Sir William Wyndham and Secretary Bromley moved for the Civil list, and that will very soon be settled. There is a matter which occasions a good deal of talk here, though people generally know very little of the matter, I mean the treaty which was on foot between the Queen and Kings of France, Spain, and Sicily. There are some in great hopes
that they may make some use of that to cast a Blame somewhere, but I don't find those who were concerned in it here under any uneasiness upon that account; it is said your Lordship has Orders to lay it before his Majesty. I hope and I don't in the least doubt but what ever your Lordship has been concerned in the more it is enquired into will the more redound to your Honour, and I wish as earnestly that nothing may happen to give any alterations to those matters you have been att so much pains in settling. We have some here who begin already to talk of a new war, but surely they must either be very ignorant of the condition of their Country or else maliciously bent upon its ruin. For my own part I don't fear such designs and therefore will trouble your Lordship no longer but only to assure you that I am, &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: August 13, 1714.

It was very kind in your Lordship to think of me in your affliction, wherein I take a very large share, without the least regard to my own interest, which I have not had leisure to think on, though busied with nothing but the melancholy thoughts of the loss of our good Princess. It is a great satisfaction to hear from your Lordship and not from flatterers, that we have so wise a Prince, able I hope to see through the malicious representations he hath been plied with, and now convinced by the unanimity that hath appeared, of the falseness of them. The Lords Justices sit very close, and I suppose doe a great deal of business. The Council have little to doe, but expect every hour to hear when the King comes. You heard I don't doubt, of the fine entry of the D. of M-. I have heard little of him since, but that he is gone to the Bath. The Dr. you mean I suppose is Arbuthnot. The lady his friend, I never made court to, which frees me from taking any notice of her now. They say the Queen was very loath to part with the late Treasurer, but was teased into it. Most of those called Tories were very warm against
him, not thinking him enough of their side, and his insincerity daily lost him ground, but some say My Lord Trevor, not Lord Bolingbroke, would have had the chief credit. The time was not fixed yesterday for the funeral. If I thought your Lordship was to come with our new King it would revive me extremely, but I doe not know what to wish, till you inform me which way you incline, for that will always be a rule to yours, &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: September 24, 1714.

The hurry of going three days to Greenwich to one so little fond of crowds as I am may be some excuse for not answering your Lordship's sooner. Now it is over, it is some pleasure to think of the bustle one lived in for that time, to so little purpose, for it is impossible the King can remember any face that was there. I am glad your Lordship had so many opportunities of speaking to him, in hopes it may have lessened some impressions so carefully given him, but here he is so beset by some people that he can only hear one side, but indeed the other's backwardness is as blameable as their
forwardness. I intended to have spoke to him, but since I see so many removes, I will let it alone, and expect my orders every hour with great resignation. I went yesterday to the Council, where the King took the oath for preservation of the Church of Scotland, and repeated the words with a better accent then I expected. Lord Chancellor Cooper made a speech in his name that you will see in print. The Prince came in and took his place in council without taking any oath.

There happened an ugly thing on Tuesday at St. James's. One Aldsworth parliament man for Windsor was insulted by Davenport, Coll. Chudleigh, and another for a Jacobite, and Chudleigh and he went out, and Mr. Aldsworth was immediately killed, which is no great wonder for he had such a weakness in both his arms, that he could not stretch them, and this from being a child, and is supposed not to be a secret to those gentlemen.

My Lord Bolingbroke is highly threatened in the Coffee houses with an impeachment, but words are but wind. My Lords Sunderland and Wharton are made amends for being left out of the list of Justices, but Secretary would have been more the inclination I fancy of the first.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, October 1, 1714.
Dear Brother,

Before this no doubt but you have heard what places have been given besides those that have been reported to be given. My Lord Orford has been said to be a going out of town dissatisfied that he had not the nomination of the lords of the Admiralty. But this day it is said he has carried his point and ordered to stay, and that he's so generous as to desire no more then the rest of them, and insists that there should be six besides himself. You have heard that the council was dissolved and to day they have named them a new. All that I inquired about was if you was left out, and I am told by one of the clerks that you were. The Bishop of London is in, but they say that's because of his great diocese here and being Bishop of all the foreign plantations.

Cadogan is declared Master of the robes, and is said will be made an Irish Lord. I was with the King a Wednesday last at Kingsenton and walked all over the Gardens with him, and after all over the lodgings, both which he liked very well. The King took us at a surprise, his coachs were ordered at three quarters of an hour warranting, but I was more ready then his Grace of Sommerset, who came before the Gold Staff which was Lord Asburnham, so that the King went alone in the coach with the Duke of Sommerset. I sent to know of the Duke if he would have me ride or go in the leading coach, as King William's Querrys did when the King did not ride himself. He sent me word I must ride, so I did, but after I was off a horse back I was every where with him. I find people are not satisfied, for the Whigs fall out among
themselves, there's not any three people hold together. The Treasury was settled to day. Lord Halifax at the head of them, he has made his nephew that's to be his heir Auditor of the Exchequor for life, but it is supposed he reserves the profits during his life. They tell a pretty extraordinary thing of Guy Poultney that he should tell his majesty that he was a man of Estate, and that he served his majesty only purely for the Honour of serving him, and that he found upon the old Estabishment that for Secretary of War there was but 1400, but upon my Lord Bullingbrook's coming to it it was made 2400, and he desired to accept it but upon the old establishment, that his M- might have a 1000 a year to gratify some body else. The King has taken him at his word and told him he should find few such men; this story he tells himself.

The Duke of A-le told me he had received a letter from you and would writ to you this post, so I shall say no more to you but in general that he assured me he had always a friendship for you. The Duke of Shrewsbury has been ill of the Gout, but was abroad to day and went before the King in Council to day.

I am sorry you did not come over with the King, for then you might not have been forgot, but if things go on as they doe you may soon be remembered. What one writs one post one is obliged to contradict the next. They say upon Sir Thomas Hanmer refusing the Chancellor of the Exchequor he has pluck't a spirit and refused Teller.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Ros, November 7, 1714.
My Lord,

I received the Honour of your Lordship's most obliging letter last night, which I would not fail to take the first opportunity to answer, though I am not able to send you the least word of news from this place; but I am going to morrow into Gloucestershire (where I design to stay some time to serve my friends att the next Elections) and I should be less able to send you anything worth the reading from thence.

I have been but little in town of late, and the Discourses I have heard in the Country from all Ranks of people are not so proper to mention in a letter, only this, that the great ground of their dissatisfaction is that they think there wants to be a proper person near the K- who might show him the true interest of the Nation, and that he has yet heard only one side. I own I heartily wish that your Lordship were in England, you cannot easily imagine of what consequence it might be, but when you consider that there has not yet been above one person of Consideration who has had any opportunity of laying the true state of matters before him, you will be more inclined to believe what I say.

The Duke of Sh- is the only man that I know that has had it in his power to talk with him of one side, and whether he has had any great opportunity, or made all the use of it that he might have done, is what I can't determine. The advantage your Lordship had of an easy conversation with him abroad, and of being Master of the Languages he speaks (which by the by has been a sad defect in some of our friends) might have had considerable effects.

You need not My Dear Lord have given me any assurance in relation to your sticking firm to your Party. I know that you have too much Honour than to leave your friends, and too much understanding not to find out the ill consequences of it. Those who have blamed every thing which has been
done abroad for these 4 years last past must in their own justification endeavour all they can to oppress the principal Actors in those affairs. And on the other hand, the Credit and reputation your Lordship has amongst the most considerable part of the Nation in number and value, is a foundation that a man who had not all your Lordship's qualifications might build something upon. One person, who might reasonably claim a great share in the credit of the Negotiations, but who always endeavoured to engross the whole, has now so entirely lost all interest with the Tory party that I can't think he can ever recover it, if he should endeavour it, but of late it has been thought that he has been more intent upon trying to get in with the other party, though with still less probability of success. I can't conclude this without telling you that I hear the M-y begin to quarrel amongst themselves, and that the party express publicly their disgust against a great D. who they say would engross all the power as he did formerly. What this may produce in time I can't tell and it is said that he has had some check from the K- himself.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, November 11, 1714.

I last night my Dear heard you were recalled which I own I could not be sorry to hear but very much the contrary. Mr. Cholmundely told Memville that you are to be a Lord of the Bed Chamber. I believe the Duchess of Shrewsbery will devour the King for she wont let any body speak to the King but herself, and the town says she rivals Madam Killmansack. I think her Grace more extrodinary in her discourse than ever. The key is at last disposed on to the Duchess of St. Albans. Baron Be has not yet been to see me nor Madam Killmunsack who I am told dos not go to Court to the Princis. Prince Kurikin has been to see me and he desired to see our daughter, and his face frittened her so that I could not make her go ne'er him. The
Venetion ambasadress has got loose from her husband and sticks close to Lord Stairs. I am jest going to dine with the Duchess of Rutland at Lord Rochester's, so can say no more but what I am entirely yours.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: August 31, 1717.

I received the honour of My Dear Lord's letter by the last post, and am sorry to find by it that your house at Boughton is so indifferent; as to the gardens being a little run to ruin, I think that of no consequence, they may be soon brought into some order. Fine groves and large rows of old elms in a fine country are invaluable things, besides in my opinion to be within a reasonable distance of London is no small consideration. I have almost a mind to make a journey on purpose to see this place to try if I can't lay a scheme of making it convenient and habitable for a small sum of money. I think you need not propose to go any further, for since you have laid out so much money att Stainborough that should still be your main seat; and indeed it is a very fine place to talk of in town, which I have heard say is the right use of a seat in the country, and since you designed it for your monument, I would (if it were my case) make no other use of it. Pardon me if I show some spleen to a place that keeps you so far from me. But raillery apart I really think Boughton should not be neglected if it can be made habitable for a moderate sum of money. There may be times when you
may enjoy that, and that you might not care to remove your family so far as Stainborough. I'll say nothing of Colston Bassett, but only that I wish it stood in Boughton Park, or if you could spare it I should have thanked you to have let me have had it att Richkings. I should have been very well satisfied with it there, and it would have saved me some money; but I don't know how you can call it a seat, unless you mean that it is a proper place to sit down att in the way to Stainborough. My notion of a good seat is where there is great parks, fine woods, and plantations, and an extensive command for all kinds of country sports in a dry soil. I think any house good enough to sleep in, and the only magnificence the country neighbours have a notion off is your strong beer and beef.

After having wrote all this stuff I need not tell your lordship that I have no manner of news to send you, it would have been inexcusable to have filled a letter in this manner if one had had anything else to have said in it, but after begging your pardon for detaining you so long to so little purpose I will conclude as shortly as sincerely that I am, &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: September 28, 1717.
My Dear Lord,

I troubled you the last time with a long letter without any news, and therefore think myself obliged to take the first opportunity to send you what I can learn. It is not unlikely the story relating to my Lord Peterborough may be in the Public papers that come out to night, but being uncertain of that I will not leave it out. I was in town last Thursday and was told there were letters from abroad giving an account that Lord Peterborough was seized att Bologna upon pretence that he had a design to murder the Pretender. The mob of the town when they heard what was the occasion of his being taken up had an inclination to fall upon him and pull him to pieces; this I suppose is inserted to show that the Pretender is very popular in Italy. The letters mention some particulars of his having Bills found about him to the value of 14,000 l. ,
and some other odd circumstances. What will the House of Lords say when they meet, to a Peer of England's being taken up on such a Pretence?

The great affair that occasions the most speculation att present is my Lord Cadogan's going into Holland. Some say it is in order to settle with the Dutch the business of the Northern Fishery, which the Government have for some time past had a project to establish, and accordingly proposals have been made for erecting a Society. It is said my Lord Cadogan has carried over a very considerable sum of money, and no doubt it must cost a great deal to bribe the Dutch to consent, who are more likely to endeavour to bribe others to stop it.

Other people say confidently that my Lord Cadogan's business is to bring the Dutch to join with us in sending a Fleet to the Mediterranean to stop the progress of the Spaniards; and others say it is to make the Duke of York Statholder. However that is, it's pretty certain that the Dutch are in no small confusion att this time.

The King of Prussia has his thoughts bent that way, and has a good large body of troops in their neighbourhood. We shall hear more of these matters when the Parliament meets, which they say will be very early. God knows what temper they will be in, for it is certain there is no better intelligence now than there was when the Parliament rose between the present and the late ministry, and it has been said that some of the latter who are now att the Bath seem to be afraid of being taken up, for the writers for the court have accused them of being in Plots with the Jacobites.

I can tell you no more upon public affairs, and perhaps you will think this little worth the trouble of reading, but however it will answer my purpose so far, I hope to draw an answer from you by which I may know how your Lordship and the rest of the family att Stainborough doe, and when you think of returning southwards.

Perhaps you have not heard an account of Lord Jersey's illness. I'm informed that he had not been in bed for almost a month before, and for one week had lived entirely upon
brandy without eating anything. He was seized att last with convulsions, and they thought he would have died immediately; he continued lightheaded a long time, and now though his fever is gone off he has his senses but by intervals. I'm afraid it is odds whether he will ever recover them entirely. Lord and Lady Landsdown came to town, but finding there was no danger as to his life, and that it would take up a long time to bring him to a perfect recovery they went back again to Longleat.
Adieu My Dear Lord, and since I have detained you so long already I won't trouble you with the ceremony of an impertinent conclusion.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Bruton? August 25, 1718.
The little expectation I had of a letter from your lordship in this remote place, was no lessening to the pleasure I had in receiving it.

It is well for me that I have not so much company to entertain, as you tell me of at Stainborough, for I should not know what to do with them. Though no body is gladder to see their friends, I am strangely at a loss with those for whom I feel nothing but indifference, but I could be tempted to envy you My Lord Dartmouth, who always inspires me with good humour, not only while I am with him but for some days after.
Besides seeing Lord Paulet twice I have conversed with very few; but those few much better then are commonly found in the country.

I can brag of very little I have done here, only the walls are covered. The hot weather has killed half my trees, and the other half escaped by force of watering. I have had no account yet of the South Sea interest being received. As soon as I do, your orders will be observed or any other you think fit to send to, &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Richskins, December 10, 1719.
My Dear Lord,

I am but just returned from a long progress, and the first news I hear is that Lady Strafford is brought to bed. I am very glad to find she is well, but I do assure you no body (except yourself) can be more concerned att the disappointment you have met with; but no more of that, you must only look upon it as one year lost, and begin again as soon as you can.

I propose to be in town on Monday, and do myself the honour to kiss your hands, but I could not let this opportunity slip of putting you in mind of an humble servant, and if you have a leisure moment one line by my servant who returns to morrow to let me know the Chart du pais would be exceedingly obliging to a poor North-Country Gentleman, who knows nothing that has passed on the South side of Trent for a month past.
I passed by Boughton and showed it to Mr. Lewis and described it's beauties, and he is much charmed with it.

I am quite confounded in my Politics, and surprised to the last degree that the Ministry should bring in the Peerage bill without a probability of carrying it. I take it for granted this Parliament will be soon up, and for good; but you will laugh att the speculations of a man who has been conversing only with country farmers. Be so charitable as to inform me a little that I may know to talk when I come to town. I won't answer for it that I think right in any one thing in the world but in this, that I shall always be, &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Richkings, August 5 1720.
My Lord,

I received your commands by my brother Ben to attend you at Stainborough. I should do it with great pleasure if I could spare time, but I have several little affairs upon my hands which will not suffer me to be so long absent
from home att present. I long to know how my mother has performed her journey, which, if she has had her health, must I'm sure? be very agreeable to her. I heartily wish I could share in your diversions att Stainborough, but all I can do is to wish that they may not be interrupted by ill health or ill weather. I'm sure everything else will be good.
I can send your Lordship no manner of news, but that the stocks have sunk a little of late; I don't know for what reason, but there is no doubt of their reviving again very soon. I am, &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, August 30, 1720.
My dear Lord,

I was in hopes your Lordship would have come up to town att this time which considering the great concerns you have in money would surely have been very proper. Mine are extremely inconsiderable in comparison to your Lordship's, and yet I find it very prejudicial to me to be long out of the way. My brother Ben is come from Richkings this morning where he brought my mother last night. They are all very well after their journey and extreme full of the enjoyments of Stainborough. I don't in the least wonder att it, for I know your Lordship can make any place agreeable, but Stainborough is in it self a very delightful place in Summer. I will not contend what it is in winter, for I reckon no place good in that season but London. Those are my present thoughts, but I won't answer how long I shall remain in those sentiments; and that I may have a place of retirement ready against I find an inclination for it, I am preparing matters in Gloucestershire to make up a Hermitage, and since your Lordship was once so good to take up a lodging with me att Paltry-town I hope I may have the honour of seeing you there when it is finished. I go into Gloucestershire next week and shall be back again before Michaelmas, and I must beg to know when I may hope to see your Lordship in town. All I can inform your Lordship of att present from hence is that there has been a hard struggle to keep the Stocks up, and if they rise after the books are shut, which is
after to-morrow, all will go well; otherwise I won't answer what will become of them. This is now the crisis, in my opinion. I don't find the Dutch doe us any great harm, the Exchange altered a little, but is now again in our favour, which is a proof as certain as any can be; but there has been considerable sums sent to Portugal, and that has been more prejudicial to our Stocks. Besides which some of the Directors have been playing the Rogue and have endeavoured to run down the stocks after having sold their own out, in order to buy in cheap again. This has putt people in a fright, and it is not so easy to bring them out again; but I expect a considerable alteration in a few days. As to the Lustering which your Lordship was merry upon in your last letter I believe our schemes are defeated. I had information from those who were in the secret and bought a good deal for the opening of the books, and if the Regency would have let them alone it would have risen prodigiously, but I think they were much in the right to knock all those bubbles on the head, and I loose nothing by it but the hopes of gain which no body can part with easier than I can; for those books I believe will never open again, unless they can make such interest with the Governor as to be sure that they shall not be prosecuted, and in that case the bargains that have been made for the opening of the Books will be beneficial enough. But for my own part I think if the great bubble can be supported that's enough for the kingdom.
We are alarmed here with the news of the spreading of the Plague in France, but as cold weather is now coming on we hope that it will secure us, otherwise we are in a great deal of danger.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: November 1, 1720.
Your kind letter My Lord was a most seasonable cordial in this melancholy time, and has given me the only agreeable moments I have felt since I came hither.

The sight of you would have given me strength to bear the
daily disappointments I meet with, a happiness I twice attempted at your house. I have so long given over my money in France that the trouble of it was almost worn out, when my subscribed annuities fell to almost nothing.

A great many flatter themselves with the king's coming, though his going did not sink the stocks, and the meeting of the parliament, but I wish it is not past their power to cure the fright that has seized every body. In the midst of these bustles, I am going to dispose of one of my daughters to My Lord Byron a disproportionable match as to their ages, but marriages not offering every day, I would not miss an opportunity, though attended with never so many inconveniences. I see so many undone people, that I comfort myself with having any thing left.
I truly rejoice that you are one of the prosperous, and wish you a long enjoyment.

The name of the place where your letter is dated is unknown to me, but I guess it in Suffolk, but not knowing the direction, this shall be sent to your house in town. My Lord Sunderland came yesterday to town.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Boughton, July 25, 1724.

I am very glad my dear life you are got safe to town. I thank God all our babes are very well, and the next good news is all the hay was got in last night; the weathere seems settled to be fine. I would not go abroad tell all the hay was in that the men might stick to it. I believe I have more employment hear than if I had been in town, for the day you went we walked a great deal, and in the evening Mrs. Briscoe came; Next day Mrs. Clark and Mr. Clarke cam and yesterday Lady Ann and I rid out in the morning, and in the afternoon Lady Erwin and Morpeth came hear. I carred them all over the gardens which they commended extremely. Mr. Methwine went from Altrope yesterday. To day we ware invited
to dinner to Sir Robert Clarke's where Mr. Isham and Mrs. Ishame met us. They pressed me mightily to stay supper (there being a moon) but William not being used to the roads I would not, though indeed he drove very carfully; we went in our flying chariot for the good of the horses. Poor Sir Robert had been out all day yesterday to get some young partridges for my supper, and as I did not stay he would make me bring them home with me. I heartily wish you had some of them; I design my love shall have his belly full if he likes them, for I could let him eat me if it would doe him good, poor baby. There was a Thursday last a horse race at Rugby in Warwickshire, and Lord Denby, Lord Craven, Sir Fuller Skipwork, and a great many more ware there, and got so drunk they ware forced to lye there that night, and the next day hired a hay cart and fourteen of them went home in it, with fiddles playing before them to Lord Denby's, and all this day guns has been going of there, that was heard at Sir Robert Clerk's. Lord Craven's brother is marred to Lady Craven's woman, though it is not yet owned publicly, but his brother has found it out. I fancy Lady Erwin is weary already of Lady Morpeth's formality, for she desired me that when I ride out I would let her know and she would come and ride with me; so a Tusday she is to come hear in the afternoon and we are to ride towards Lord Northampton's, and if they are not come down we are to see the house and chase. This is all the news I can tell you at present. I am glad to here Lady Wentworth is better; I beg my humble duty to her, and am, my dear Life, ever yours most truly.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Boughton, August 3, 1724.

note.value: PASSAGE OMITTED

text.p:
I never knew the cook so sober and quiet as he has been ever since you went, and he dressed the dinner perfectly
well when L. Erwin dined hear. The hamper of wine I sopose will be at Northampton to morrow, and I'll send for it; as to white wine there is three bottles of the white port left that came from London, for a pint is the most I use in a day, and very often a pint sarves two days. I want to know what you would have me doe about Lady Pomfret's geese. Lord Wentworth and the girls I thank God are perfectly well, and Lord Wentworth is grown very fond of me which makes me very happy. He comes every morning to eat his breakfast by me; I thank God he eats very heartily five times a day. Lord Northampton's family came down a Saturday and Lady Halifax comes down to day to stay for three weeks. We dined to day at Sir Jus Isham's and there was a very handsome dinner; Mrs. Clark was there but Sir Justin was not well enough to dine with us. I design to go to morrow to Lady Morpeth's for Lady Morpeth has been hear once and Lady Erwin three times since you went. A Dieue my dear Life and soul all happiness ever attend you.

note.value: FROM LADY LUCY WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: November 17, 1724.
Dear Pappa,

I hope your Lordship will excuse this being the first that ever I write in my life and i hope you will come hither
soon for the country is very dull without your good company pray give my duty to my grand momma i am dear pappa your,
most affectionate and most dutiful Daughter
Lucy Wentworth.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, January 25, 1726.
Dear Brother,

According to my promise I send you the sequel of the debate in the house of Lords. After Lord Townsend had done speaking then the Duke of Rutland got up and said two or three words by way of form to third the Address; then Lord Bathurst got up and said his fears of a war was increased since he had heard what Lord Townsend said in expassiating upon the ingratitude of the Emperor who was sounding the alarm every where to battle, and as one lord had taken notice of the mismanagement of the last war, he would of the ill management of the ministry of the money in a long peace, which made us not in so good a condition as we should be to enter into a new war; and he was for Englishmen warding off the insults and menaces of Foreign Powers not only with words but blows. He had not in the least any distrust of the King, but of his ministry he confessed he had, and that it was the right of every member of parliament to find fault with them. He thought there was no occasion to have any mention made of the Pretender to rease
any fears in the minds of people about him, when all agreed his was an expiring interest, and he could have agreed that those words might stand part of the address, but not his Perjured adherents , which was a sort of calling names to no purpose. Then Lord Falmouth got up and said he never did fear the Pretender, nor did not now, and believed he never should until he should see one that had been a minister of his a minister here, and then the Pretender was to be dreaded by everybody; and then he laughed to those lords that set by him, and told them he had nick Bat. for his friend Be . Here was an end of the debate; the address was carried as you see without any devition. It was thought in town that all things were agreed upon with Mr. Poultney and the ministry, but he seemed in very good earness when he spoke things he thought reflected by Sir R. Walpoole, who answered him very well with a great deal of deliberation and temper, there had been above four millions paid and a sinking is still going on. The war we had with the Spainards was before his time and none of his advising; for every thing that happen in his time he could answer when called upon. But as for my friend Horace, he made but sad work, and gave Shippen an opportunity of bantering the great Ambassador; to be sure the Hanover Treaty as he called it could not be made to protect any of his Germain dominions, for the Act of Settlement had provided in very strong words that the English should have nothing to do. Lord Finch said it might be called the Hanover Treaty from the place it was dated, but there was done nothing but purely for the interest of England, Hungerford had an opportunity to croak a joke on the Knights of the Bath. Sir Robert Sutton being the first that moved for the address, when H- had a mind to answer something Sir R. S- had said, without naming him he said he had difficulty how to describe him, and, looking about the house, said he spied many adorned like him, and at last called him the member with the badge. Every thing goes
very well, and since the Commons comes so heartily in to give the Supply there's no fear any foreign Power dare invade us.

I am told the Duke of Warton is one of the Perjured adherents meant. He has been very busy at Vienna, informing them of the state of the nation, which if true is horrid for any Englishman to be guilty of. A man may be disobliged by some particular People, but that he should carry his resentment so far, as to do anything that might tend to the ruin of his country .

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, May 26, 1729.
Dear Pappa,

I should be very glad to hear you was pleased with my letter. I have obeyed your command in walking in the perk
every day. I believe my sisters designs to write to you. I hope I shall see you in a short time at London again. My mama is gone to Chelsea. To day and yesterday she walked with the Queen and was ready to drop down she was so weary. Excuse my bad writing; so I am your most affectionate and most dutiful son
Wentworth.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, May 25, 1730.
Dear Papa,

We walked in the Park last night, their was a great deal of company, Lady Bab Mansel, Lady Grace Vane, Lady
Betty Lowher and a Miss Bolder, Mrs. night, Mr. Meados, Mr. Conaley, Count Nasa, Lord John Murry, and we saw Lady They Spencer, Lady Bab North, Lady Catherine Noel and Miss Mountague looking over the wall. My sesters give their duty to you. I am, &c.

note.value: FROM LORD WILLIAM BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Bruton, October 12, 1730.

I cannot make the excuse of business where I have so little, for no sooner acknowledging your Lordship's most kind entertaining letter I am ashamed to name the date, but you were pleased to tell me of so many places you intended going to, that it was impossible to fix upon any for a direction, before your removal to London, not to be avoided I suppose since it is law business that calls. I am sorry for the occasion, which I always dreaded, chiefly for the tediousness. Your Lordship will have full time to follow it, since the parliament is not likely to meet soon, and I wish you well at the end of your travels, as they call it in Westminster hall.

My Lord your fine house is put in a frame, and I walk over your walks some times till I fancy I hear the cascades. No place is worth any thing without wood and water; these I find Stainborow abounds in. There is nothing more pleasant than seeing fine seats, but they are very thin strewn here about. I went a year ago to see a famous house of Mr. Dorrington's, a vast heap of stones that has the look of a great hospital. Naming My Lord Huntington, I have heard a fine description of his park; your Lordship who has bin there, can judge whether it answers. We have had a fine autumn, don't you regret leaving the country so soon. I can only write of the weather for I seldom see any body out of the house; and for news, no body will vouchsafe to send any. I desire none better than of your health and ease in body and mind, for your Lordship has not in the world a truer well wisher than, &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: December 12, 1730.
Dear Papa,

I have no news to tell you but Mr. Southwell is dead. Pray Papa, give my duty to Lord Bathirst and my service to Lady Bathirst. Monswer I believe is gone to France for he sent for his Trink to the kings arms and was ready in a hackney coach and toke in in to him and bid them drif a way to jerin cross. This Letter is of my one spilling. I am Dear Papa
Your most affectionate and most dutiful son
Wentworth.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD
DECEMBER, 1730.

text.p: Dear Papa,
