Master Wallpole came to me last night wee played at Quadarill and I won 10 pence at a penny a fish. The day before yesterday we went to Lord Holderness and Lady Carolina Darcey. I hope I shall see you soon in London. My cousin Lee has sent me the dor-mice. We have had very good weather hear - I hope you have had the same: this Letter is of my one Spilling: I am, &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, December 26, 1730.
Dear Papa,

Master Wallpole was to see me yesterday. Lord and Lady Pomfret is come to town. Duke and Duss of Devonshire is gone out of Town to keep their Chirstmas in the country. We have writ a great many Letters and directed them to cirencester. We was in as great a fright as you cold be for fear you should be sick in hearing from you . Lord and Lady Oxford is not come to town yet; my cousin
handborought is at bath and desings to make to much of you, she says that she has eenquired where is the best clarit and has provided as warm a room as she has in her house; my cousin Lee has sent me the Dor-mous But it is dead. The old Dor-mous is very well and in perfect good health. Lord Delorain and Mrs. Witworth are both dead of a fit of an Appoplex: I have teared you long enough with my silly scroll. I am, &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, May 27, 1731.
Dear Papa,

My mama and Lady Anne went to a Ball at Lord Mayor's, you was envieted. There was Lord and Lady Oxford and Lady Marget Harley, Duchess of Briegwater and Mr. Conaley, the Earl of Rothes, Mr. Morgin Vane, Lord and Lady Essex and Lady Betty Nightingale, Lady Atkins and Miss Pig Stonhouse and Lord Gore after them, and Lord and Lady Lichfeild, Mrs. Menal, Miss Bartey and Mr. Herbert, Mr. Fredrick and Mr. Jack ditto, Lord and Lady Brickshire and Lord Andover. Pray, Papa, give my service to Mr. Lee. I am, &c.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, May 27, 1731.

I had my Dearest the pleasure yesterday of yours of the 24th, and am glad you are so well. I thank God our jewel and the girls are perfectly so. I believe by this time you don't complain of the weathere being so hot, for yesterday and to-day is as cold as winter. Lady Ann was very happy at Lord Mayor's ball; She says she wishes this Lord Mayor was like Whittington. The supper was very fine, he seemed very sorry he had not your company. The Ladies was Duchess Bridgwater, Lady Berkshire, Lady Lichfeild, Lady Oxford, Lady M. Harly, Lady Betty Nightingale, Miss Lawson, Lady Atkins, Mrs. Stonhouse, Mrs. Menell, Mrs. Cottons, and Mrs. Lockwood. The men, Lord Berkshire,
Lord Essex, Lord Lichfeild, Lord Oxford, Lord Gower, Lord Rothes, Lord Duplin, Mr. Vane, Mr. Conely, Mr. Fredericks, Lord Andover, Mr. Jefferys and Mr. Lisle. The Duchess of Leeds has taken a lodging in Garman Street and cam to it last night. Some day this week the Duke of Devonshire is to give a very fine entertainment at some famous house, the company that is asked is the Duchess of Marlborough, Dowerger Lady Burlington, Mr. and Mrs. Hanbery and myself. The Prince supps in town almost every night with some of his ladies, last night it was at Lady Hillsborough's, but by what I hear there is at these suppers hardly enough to fill their bellies. No body sees any thing of the King and Queen. A Dieue my Dearest ever yours.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, July 1, 1731.
Dear Brother,

Tuesday there was an order for a battalion of the Guards to march by Friday next for Portsmouth, to go on board the Fleet that's to carry Don Carlos to Italy, that our fleet may be well manned in case we should meet with any French fleet by the way, that should have a mind to speak to us. Don Carlos is to be aboard our Admiral, that we may command the Spanish ships that goes with us; that expedient was found out, to make the Spaniard wave their insolent demand to command us. These orders to the Guards were kept as secret as they could, in order for to job in the city , but yesterday the orders that are given out, for all the horse and dragoons to march to the Kentish and Sussex shore, has alarmed every body, but I don't find stocks are fallen yet. We know the French have marched 25 battalion to Dunkirk, and are fitting out a great fleet; they say we have broke the Treaty of Utrech, and they are at liberty to fortify Dunkirk publicly; and that we may not pretend to hinder them they will have a fleet out before the town. We hear nothing yet of any transports but if we should neglect to guard our coast
that would be soon had. I find the people in general are glad to have a stroke with the French, but how the people at the helm are disposed I know not, but do not doubt but they will take the best and wisest course, for the honour and safety of the nation.

I have not been at court since I knew of Mrs. H- being Countess of Suffolk, but by some gentlemen I hear she's so well pleased that she hears better already. In the Prints it is said she's made Groom of the Stole to the Queen, for out of the Bedchamber it seems it is resolved she shall not go. I heard that my Lord Suffolk had arrested the body of the late Lord, but what he means by that I know not, nor could the person that told me the news tell me.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Hampton Court, July 26, 1731.
Dear Brother,

I am very glad any thing I can write can be agreeable to you. As to what you want to know, the same uncertainty remains for the King has not yet declared he will not go, but as no orders are yet given for his going, I think it certain he will not. About three weeks ago the Prince betted Johny Lumley 20 guineas to 10 the king would go; I should be glad his highness would take now my two or three to one he did not go. Friday day last when I gave the Queen my memorial, she gave me an opportunity to put the Question slyly to her, but she gave me no answer but a smile; she asked me where you was now, I told her in Yorkshire, in great expectation of seeing the King and her Majesty there, but as to the memorial I had the answer desired, when she had read it, she said I should have it, she would speak to Sir Robert and gave it me again biding me give it her again when Sir R. came, if she keep't it might be mislaid. My Wife and Son I know will reckon all this nothing. I know as well as they that it is a long time to Christmas, and that many things happen between the Cup and the Lip, yet I am resolved to be such a fool to be pleased till the time comes. I took
occasion when I got her alone with the Duke and young Princesses, coming to the first door, she comes out into the Garden, and had a good long limping walk with her before we came to the usual place of waiting where all the company meets at her going into the chaise. Saturday last I carried a coach full of Ladies in a coach and six, to Sir John Charter who has treated the Prince with two balls; the first women were the neighbouring country farmers daughters and his servant maids, the next were Lord Hallifax's daughters, and ladies the Prince had named. They talk Mr. Poultney is to be impeach't as soon as the Parliament meets. I heard Sir Wm. Young say they had reported he was gone to Northfolk to give Sir Robert an account of Franklin's trial, but he had staid in London until he came here; he sat next to Lord Winchelsea, whose countenance was much cast down till the trial was put off. I am a diligent, sober attendant at Court so havn't much time to write.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Hampton Court, August 3, 1731.
Dear Brother,

Upon the Death of Mr. Low, several people tells me you have a fair opportunity to make me a Member of the house of Commons. I tell them it is what I don't desire, and keep the true reason to myself that if there's any money to be spent you will not do it for me, I fear; but since there's a bill past that no money is to be spent, I have some small hopes you'll try it for me. I am sure it will turn to both our advantages, for I see nobody is so much minded as Members at Court. You asked me in one of your letters if I could have any serious discourse with Sir Robert Walpole; the setting me up for Alborough, though I did not succeed, would give me an opportunity of creating an intimacy with him, the talking to him of the intentions you had for me, would show you esteemed me, and by that means I might be more regarded
by him. I could likewise tell the Queen I would undergo the fatigue purely to serve her and the R. F. The business of the house would be far from a fatigue to me, for it would be a pleasure, you know I have often crowded into the house when I had no business, and I should not be so preposterous to neglect it when I had, and if I had not made a full resolution never to be concerned in liquor again, having full employment in business would keep me from it. My Lord Grantham, who was one of the idle tattlers against me, told me yesterday that he had observed me ever since I came here I had been very sober, and wished me joy. I thanked his Lordship and told him as I had promised the Queen so I would him, that he nor no man should see me the least concern in drink, that as by the Queen's goodness to me I had some prospect of having my affairs easier, I should have no occasion to drown and stupefy my thoughts. You may remember when Coll. Negus proposed to you in the late King's Reign, to bring me into Parliament, he would get me 500 l. from Court, and if there was any occasion for it I don't doubt but I could get the same sum now, but it would be better if it could be done without troubling them for money, and show your interest the greater. If you don't approve of me for your member, I should be glad you would use your interest for my son, who is a very sober man, and will make a very good Member of Parliament, but as I have more experience I have the vanity to think I should make as good a one. I beg the favour of your thoughts and answer soon, for till I hear from you I shall do nothing but think of it.

The news of the Peace is as we could wish, and Sir Robert will not prove such a blunder as some people would make him. Franklin reckons he has obtained another Victory, for when he had given bail, the Attorney General proposed he should be bound to his good behaviour, but Lord Raymond said that until he was found guilty, in the Eye of the law Mr. Franklin was an innocent man, and therefore could not bind him to his good Behaviour.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: January 15, 1732.
My Lord,

I have signed and sealed the proxy. You'll be pleased to date it, for I believe it should be after the meeting of the parliament. I can hardly think you will have divisions near enough to call for proxies. It is a great pleasure to hear of your lordship and your? constancy to your friends. You
love journeys and I live in hopes of your taking a progress again westward, the road is a bowling green in comparison of Leicestershire and Northamptonshire. When I go into the north it shall be to see Stainborow; everything else will be but accessory. I have not seen Pope's verses. These people are all flattery or abuse. They put me in mind of some who cannot be civil to one body without affronting the rest of the company. Mr. Trevanion told truth of his often hearing from hence, but it is the sisters keep the correspondence. I seldom write to my daughter, though I love her entirely and she deserves it. All here are proud of being remembered, and I am &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: February 3, 1733.
My Lord,

Of all the privileges of the noble house there is none I like better than proxies, since it brings me the happiness
of a letter from your lordship, and the pleasure of knowing you are recovered of the pernicious cold that spares so few at London. I hope there is not the least feeling left of the accident in Yorkshire. I don't imagine numbers will ever come so near as to call for proxies, but in all events I always think my self safe in my Lord Strafforde's hands, though I expect to be miserably defeated in the Army bill. The noise made about excises will I fear bring the load again upon land. They talk as if excises were a new thing, when almost every is so already and no care to prevent retailers raising the prices at the same time. My daughter would have bin proud of your lordship's notice; I do not wonder you should not know her, for I hardly recollect her myself. What with children and an old husband she has quite lost her youth. The town is highly obliged by your assembly after a great dejection for the loss of the Duke of Norfolk's. As I am one of your oldest acquaintance I will venture to say there is none wishes you better, nor is more truly yours, &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, March 29, 1733.
Dear Papa,

I hope by this time you are in good health at Suffolk. We was last night at the Duke of Devonshire, it was a ball, their was 8 couple, viz. Lady Coroline Cavendish and Lord Sunbury, Lord Heartington and Lady Mary Montague, Lord Conoway and Lady Harriet, Mr. Walpole and Lady Lucy, Mr. Conoway and Miss Wortley, a Mr. Webster and Lady Dorothy, Mr. Whitworth and Lady Betty Cavendish, me and Lady Betty Montague; and we had a very handsome supper, viz. at the upper end cold chikens, next to that a dish of cake parched almonds sap biscuits , next to that a dish of tarts and cheescakes, next to that a great custard, and next to that another dish of biscuits parched almonds and preserved apricots, and next a quarter of lamb. I hopy Ody and Ratty is very well. I am, &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Cirencester, August 15, 1733.
My dear Lord,

I ought to have wrote to you before this time to have condoled with your lordship upon the death of my aunt, but I have been in such a perpetual hurry ever since, that I have not had a moment's time. I don't know what is to be said upon such an occasion, for though she seemed likely to live some years
still, when I had the honour to see her last, yet it did not appear to be a life very desirable, she being so far advanced in years.

I hope your lordship and all your family are in good health; for my part I have not time to be sick, for having the rage of elections upon me at this time, I can think of nothing else. I have set up my son for the county here, and it had like to have been without any opposition, but the contrary party would not submit at first to a compromise, and now Mr. Chester is joined with my son we will not agree to a peace, and I believe indeed we shall carry it for both. We have at last brought it about that my brother Ben shall have an easy election at Gloster, and we are very secure of Ciceter; but the entertaining a whole county is not only pretty troublesome, but is attended with some small expense. I hope this will excuse me for not paying my compliments to your lordship sooner, and I shall trouble you no farther now but to assure you that I am, &c.

note.value: FROM GEORGE PHIPPS TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: November 17, 1733.
My noble Lord.

I believe I told your lordship that Mr. Wortley was att Leeds, and on Monday night next Sir Miles, Sir John Bland, Mr. Fox, Sir John Kay, Mr. Wortley and several other gentlemen are to meet att Sheffield and drive there the next day, to go about the town to get votes. I believe that we shall have the worst success in Sheffield of any town in Yorkshire; but I hope not so bad as people imagine.
I find that no other person is to be put up with Sir Miles, but my opinion is that two against two would have been better. Mr. Travis is to go to Sheffield to be in the cavilcade for Mr. Wortley.

I am afraid that the cause will starve for want of money, and several votes will be lost for a small matter of treating. I will do what I can for the cause but a method should be concluded of, which way money may be raised to give some small matters of money for meat and drink to those who are really poor and cannot afford to go without.
There was eight aldermen and the mayor att Leeds for Sir Miles, and every person paid his proportion, so Sir Miles was only his share .
Lord Milton and Jessop was att Sheffield last Tuesday, and gave a treat, but I don't know as yet how much it cost them, but I can know.
The whole number of votes in Leeds 250
Single votes for Sir Miles 158
Half votes for Sir Miles 36
Persons not home so can't tell for who 30
Denied Sir Miles 25
I am now with Mr. Wortley and we are sending messengers about to invite gentlemen to the meeting at Sheffield; and I am &c.

note.value: FROM GEORGE PHIPPS TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: December 1, 1733.
My Noble Lord.
As to elections going on I find the hearts of the people to be mostly inclined to Sir Miles. I look upon it that the other party must buy a great many if they carry in any great numbers.

I think if Mr. Wortley would set up it would be one way to secure Sir Miles, by breaking Lord Malton's interest in our quarter. But if Lord Burlington stands fast, and considering who is for us that was against us the last election, it will be easy to carry two against Sir Rowland and Turner, especially by laying out a little money northward about Sedborrow or thereabouts where are great numbers of freeholds, but att such a distance they will not come, unless something be given towards their charges.
Lady Londonderry has the command of several votes att both Cudworth and att Bolton, if your lordship would pleasure to secure them, and I will speak the freeholds.

note.value: FROM GEORGE PHIPPS TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: December 18, 1733.
My Noble Lord,

I postponed in expectation to hear some particular accounts from the north of Sir Miles's success there. Sir Miles desired we would write to him how votes stand, and we shoud hear from them; but no account is come, only one letter from Mr. Robinson, Lord Thanett steward, who writes to Mr. Fenton to take care of Bolster Stone votes, and
further says that without boasting with them there are 40 to one for Sir Miles.

We increase our votes here upon which we have lately had a very sufficient proof by Lord Malton's making a counter march upon us att Sheffield which was done by the advice of Mr. Shore &c., who told Lord Milton that if another treat was made att Sheffield those votes Sir Miles had got would come over to his lordship again; so on Wednesday last they came to Sheffield to treat with wine. And in answer to this there is a gent. that lives near Sheffield who's name is Bampford, of estate about 800 l. per annum , not married, about 23 years of age, one of Samll Fleming's sons is his steward, who espouses Sir Miles's interest; I have been with him att several places. So Mr. Bampford hearing of Lord Malton's design went to Sheffield that day, and likewise sent for me to meett him, but I was gone to Barnsley to end the affair of Fenton and Morton which I did. But I went the next morning to Sheffield to see how matters stood, where I found Mr. Bampford who had been treating Sir Miles's men with ale only, and their numbers had increased 5 for Sir Miles, who all sign a paper to stand fast and true, so that we hope to have a balance against their molten images; we do very well and much better then could be expected. Sir Tho. Sanderson, if he gives Sir Miles his interest he will cramp Lord M- on that side. I can't find Lord M- interest is anything like the last time, I think half will not be carried in by him as was then.
Lord M- servant who went to treat this time att Sheffield told Lord M- that the money would be spent in vain which prove so.
We have not been at Rotheram yett, only Mr. Bamford and I is to go.

I humbly conceive by your lordship's letter that as to some money towards managing the election that I levelled particularly att your lordship. I meant the whole body att a general meeting, which should be as soon as could be. Mr. Wortley bore Mr. Traviss charges and mine and furnished
me with some money to spend att some other places; those on the place are always actors.

I don't think what has been spent is any thing considerable by any that has attended Sir Miles. I believe Bampford has spent as much as any. Lady Win brings everything about this election up to a quarrel. Mr. Mattw Wentworth who designs to stand for the register office went to ask Sir Rowland to give him leave to stand neuter, which Lady Win resented so much that when Mr. Matt. Wentworth was going away she sent a servant after him to desire him to come no more there, which has displeased all Matt. Wentworth's friends. Lady Win was ridiculing a gentlewoman in York, and the lady was present unknown to Lady Win; but the gentlewoman fell upon her ladyship so warmely that Lady Win made her exit. These things doe Sir Rowland harm. Sir Rowland told Justice Norton that he would have the Election or it should cost him dear, upon which Horton said 'take notice, gentlemen, a man that will buy his country will sell it, so I hope no wise person give Sir Rowland his vote, and I now tell Sir Rowland I will make all the interest I can for Sir Miles.'

I tell people Geneva is a dangerous liquor, and Sir Rowland was edducated there. I do what ever I can. I hear for truth that there are several gent. that are upon Sir Rowland's side who says that they will have Sir Rowland swore before they give their votes that he will not vote for any excise. Sir Tho. Sanderson has 96 votes in Tickhill which Lord Milton had the last time.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, January 3, 1734.
Dear Papa,

I went yesterday with my uncle and Monsieur Baud to see the great man, I never saw such a monster, he is eight foot and three inches high, he is a Suiedish or Polish man, he was dressed like the Algerinains ambassadors, his waistcoat was yellow with gold loops and a robe of scarlet velvet or damask laced round with gold and a turbaned on is head, he lives at Mr. Burleighs in charing cross; and after that I went to see my Lord Deerhurst and I saw my Lord
Coventry. They say Princess was married the day before yesterday in private, and that they do not own it till he comes from the Bath.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, January 5, 1734.

I was very glad my Dearest to hear by your letter to my love and Hamilton that you ware got safe as far as Ipswich. I thank God my Royal Rose and the girls are perfectly well. We had last night and this morning a great deal of snow, but it thaws as it falls. L. Anne Harvey invited my love and I yesterday to a fat Pig and two Partridge, which my Jewel eat very well of. The Queen, Princess Royal, and Duke of Marlborough christened Lord Portmore's daughter last night, the Chelsey Duchess of Rutland did the honours. We received this week from Wentworth Castle, half a doe, a turkey, 2 pullets, 2 partridges and a woodcock, and 2 bottles of ale for you. Mrs. Duncomb of Yorkshire was here a Thursday, she tells me Sir John Kaye has declared he'll stand for York city. I told her I heard Mr. Duncomb was to join with him, but she said she could not tell, for he thought it time enough to declare. She makes sad complaints of Versally, she says he's gon away and they can't tell what is become of him, and has left all their hall in rubish. We had a good deal of company a Thursday; the Bank won 60 l. , there was no English played but L. Crew, Sir R. Rich, and Lord Chessterfield's brother, who I fancy lost the most. I was yesterday at Buckingham House, Mr. Caesar was there and railed extremely against the Court, but the Duchess did not in the least enter into the conversation but rathere took their part; and when he was gon she told me she hoped I took notice she gave him little or no answer. Lady Bullinbroke is dying. My brother calls often to see me, but he has told me no news. My love was yesterday to return Lord Granby's viset and they had a party at Codrell, which was
Lord Granby, Lord Dalketh, Lord Robert and Lord Wentworth, and my poor love lost half a crown - a Dieue my Dear ever yours.

note.value: FROM LADY ANNE STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, January 8, 1734.

I received my Dearest yours of the 3rd last night and you may be sure am happy to hear you are so well. I thank God my Royal Rose and the girls are extremely so, and yesterday he walked round the Park; a Sunday I carred him to court with me, and whilst I was at church my brother took care of him and showed him all the rooms at St. James, and when the Queen cam in he made his bows very handsomely A great many of the Foreigners (my brother says) talked to him and said he spoke french perfectly well. My love says he likes going to court better of a Sunday than any day. We ware yesterday at court; they thought in the morning they should have had no hazard for want of players, but at last they got the D. of Graffton, Lord Harrington, Mr. Shutzes and Lady Betty Garmain, which was all besides the K., Q., Prince and Princess Royal. There was a ball, but it was sad company in the great drawing, but there was a room kept for the Prince and his company, and when he was going to dance he cam up and said he hoped he should have Lady Lucy's company in his set, and he was sorry Lady Anne Conolly was not there too, for he had a great deal of pleasure in the company of me and my family; and he asked Lucy if she had got a partner, for if she had not he would get her one, but Mr. John Bosscowin had asked her. The Prince danced with Lady Bab Mansell. I hope Wardman will com to London, if he does he shall see an opera and all the Royal family. Lady Kaye showed me a letter from Leeds that says every thing goes well for Sir Miles Stapleton. We have terrible cold weathere here and I fancy we shall have snow. I wish you would ask Wardman, if we should want Molly Wood in town, if he knows of any maid Mrs. Wardman could get that would be fit for Wentworth Castle; for Nanny Downing is such an nasty - I must be as bad as mothere Needham to keep her.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: January 26, 1734.
My Lord,
What a support in life the kind remembrance is of a valuable friend, is easier felt then expressed. The marks of constancy I receive from your Lordship renews the pleasures of our first acquaintance.

My Lord Bruce in expectation of strong debates at the first meeting sent me a messenger with a proxy. My answer you saw. My Lord Henton's calling up has put an end to a disagreeable struggle. Daughters are no burden to My Lord Carteret. It is not the only instance of his good luck. The loss of one who did the part of a mother to mine so many years has nearly touched me in this remote corner, her company will be missed, though for my own particular, London would be a solitude, where most of my acquaintance are gone and the time past for making new. I must ever be, My Lord your Lordship's most humble and most obedient servant.

note.value: FROM RICHARD WARDMAN TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Wentworth Castle, March 12, 1734.
My Lord,

As this day is Sunday I galloped over to Wakefield to see what time Mr. Fox and Mr. Wentworth voters was to meet, and the day; so it is set out for next Wedinsday morning at six a clock; and I called upon Mr. Wentworth of Woley in my way home, and he told me the same. And we are to join Mr. Wortley and Mr. Traviss with their company at Tadcaster the same day, and so go all together in to the City of York; which I hope will bee the greatest number of men and a greater show then the Ribin and Black Coats can make. Mr. Phipps we know him and so dus all mankind that ever see him, and his great talent is of braging and telling of lies so that nobody minds him, nor, if your lordship will believe me, he is not much taken notice off by no body; but I think your lordship not putting him in to no power he will bee out of temper, for he did expect to have seen your lordship in Yorkshire, for I always told him that I expected your lordship every day. As to horses for the voters we must let them that wants have some from our tenants, for Mr. Wortley has got one hundred horses off his tenants and other people and gives 12 pence a day for them, so I must get one of some of our tenants for old Rook.
Mr. Wentworth of Wooley has sent 70 pounds to help Mr. Bamforth with his men, and they want to know what Mr. Wortley will do, for he has not declared his mind yet.

note.value: FROM RICHARD WARDMAN TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Wentworth Castle, April 20, 1734.
My Lord,

I received your lordship's letter of the 16th. As there will be a meeting of a great many gentlemen at York the 26th to consider how to bring in their men at proper times, and to consult with Sir Miles to do every thing for his interest, and with all to save their money; so tell that day is over we
can't judge the time or day our country men must go into York. I was sent for to Silkson yesterday by Mr. Fenton and Mr. Walker to give a small treat to some freeholders and we spent five shillings apiece, and Mr. Fenton thinks that if we had a meeting at Barnsley before Lord Milton comes down that with spending your lordship a ginney or two might spirit them up again; for since the Post Office is not got my Lord Milton is not much looked upon amongst them, but they are all riding about and does not leave a stone unturned, for we doe think hear that their hearts fails them, and if due care be taken of Sir Miles men Sir Rowland must loose it. Your lordship and Mr. Wortley has been expected very much in Yorkshire about this election. If Mr. Wortley had known of the meeting at York very likely he would have gon; if he does not com down our interest about Sheffield will sink, for Mr. Bomforth is not able to support the charge, and what advice to give your lordship about spending your money I am not wise enough to judge; but a little at Barnsley and at Wakefield would look well, and the world would see your lordship did doe great things and stir about. It is thought Mr. Spencer does not spend his money freely nor does not take much pains; and indeed if your lordship do join with Mr. Wortley they will expect you to join your purse with him, for that is the chief thing our country gentlemen wants your lordship and Mr. Wortley to bee at the most expense. If your lordship would have me go over to York, or Mr. Traviss, perhaps they will be bringing one in for such and such towns in the weapon tacks to take care of the men belonging to those places; but I will not pretend anything without your lordship's orders &c.

note.value: FROM RICHARD WARDMAN TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Wentworth Castle, May 5, 1734.
My Lord,

I received your lordship's letter dated the 2nd instant, and a whole sheet of paper pays no more post than half a
sheet, so I hope to fill this sheet before I have dun writing. Every letter I have from your lordship costs 7 pence. The first thing I shall begin with is - elections. Last Thursday we had a great meeting at Barnsley, the great Mr. Wortley, Mr. Wentworth of Wooley, and some gentlemen from Sheffield and Darfield. Mr. Wentworth sent for me and Mr. Travis and we went all over the town of Barnsley, and I hope we got the better half of the voters. We had a good diner and every one paid their shares and then parted, and to-morrow Mr. Wortley and Mr. Wentworth goes to Sheffield, and laid their commands of Mr. Travis and me to meet them their. So Mr. Travis and I have considerd that he shall go and I stay at home, for its of a Monday and a good excuse for me, it being our sale day in the woods.

This time of election will soon bee hear, and I cannot write to your lordship above once or twice before it begin, and shut be glad to have your orders about the tenants and other people that is for your lordship interest. Abraham Rock he will want a horse, and two more at Barnsley that will want horses. It will bee of great expense if your lordship was to treat those people yourself and yeet more I doubt if you was to make a purse with Mr. Wortley or Mr. Wentworth. Mr. Travis will go with all your tenants and friends about Wentworth Castle and Barnsley at the time when Mr. Wortley and Mr. Wentworth goes, and that will bee of the 15th instant; and I believe that very day all Wakefield that is for Sir Miles goes. Their is an old man they call Johnson your lordship tenant that lives at Wakefield, he will want a horse to York; or else I think they are all rich enough at Wakefield too bear their oune expenses. Mr. Travis I doubt will want money, but he is modest and dus not say any thing; I am afraid his tenant dus but pay him badly. We both appear for your lordship, and is as sparing and as careful as we can, and what orders your lordship gives us we shall take care not to exceed.

Yesterday after the other parties had heard so many gentlemen had been for Sir Miles, came Sir Rowland Win and all his crew of people too Barnsley, and a great diner at Tom Hacksworth's, but we had ours at your lordship's inn at
Roper's; but we had a great dale of better gentlemen, but they was more freer of their money, and spent a great dale more money then we did; and I doubt got one or two of our men that had promised us. Mr. Wortley takes a great dale of pains about this affair, and this day a great many gentlemen is to dine with him at the Lodge. Just now Mr. Wentworth of Wolly called hear to know how your lordship did, and with his humble servis to your lordship. So he is gon to dine at Mr. Wortley's; and so goes to Sheffield to morrow to make what interest they can for Sir Miles; but I doubt my Lord Milton purse strings opens more easily then theirs will do, and he has sent and been at Sheffield before them, for he dus not spear his money, and I think he will bring in Sir Rowland at last, for it is thought they begin to get men of us now - so much for elections.

note.value: FROM GEORGE PHIPPS TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My noble Lord,

Mr. Wortley is very hot for Sir Miles, and has not rested one day but Saturday last. On Thursday we went to Barnsley and was met by Mr. Wentworth of Wooley, Mr. Nevile of Chevett, Mr. Beamont of Darton, Mr. Fenton and several others, and we had great success. Sir Rowland came to Barnsley on Saturday, upon which a great part of the voters left the town. On Friday we went unto Handsworth parish and some adjacent towns. Mr. Bampford attended, Mr. Stacie of Balyfield, Mr. Williams and several others. This parish joins Eckington parish where Mr. Griffith lives and pretends great interest there; but we find ours much superior for Sir Miles. This day we are att Sheffield with Mr. Wentworth and the same gentlemen who dined with Mr. Wortley yesterday; with a further addition of gentlemen, Mr. Wrightson and others, we shall run them hard; but not without hopes of carrying a majority. But where we go next it will be considered of this night.
There has been a large subscription att York, and some of the money sent to Mr. Bampford, for a great part of the poorer sort must have horses sent, &c. or they can't go.
Mr. Wrightson tells me that an express is just comed in to Mr. Nevill to acquaint him that Sir William Milner has declined the pole at York, so Sir John Kay must be chose with Mr. Tompson.

The gentlemen wishes that your lordship's affairs would allow your lordship so much time as to take a step into Yorkshire before the election. It is supposed that either Turner or Win will give up before the election. But I take this to be only grounded upon Milner's giving up at York. Lord Milton went to York yesterday to meet gentlemen upon Turner's and Winne's account to settle the time of their men's coming into York. I find by reports in the country that person is afraid of being mobbed; he has put all his own servants into new liveries, and the old ones he has put upon farmer's sons, so he is double maned. Sheffield mob huzzaed Mr. Jessop out of the town last night, 'Sir Miles for ever and no Excise,' but could not quiet them but followed to the end of the town. I am glad to hear Mr. Conolly is choose and that Northampton election went so well.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My Dear Lord,

I received the Honour of your Lordship's by the last post, and am much obliged to you for the goodness you are pleased to express in it to me and my family. I have had enough of Elections for this time, and shall leave Mr. Wodehouse to fight his Battle himself; I have secured him a retreat here, in case of a defeat. I think he can expect nothing else, for I take it for granted the Norfolk Election must be carried (one way or other) as the great Man would have it.

If your Lordship has a leisure hour I should be glad to hear how matters go in the Great world particularly as to
foreign affairs. I think no more of Elections, only I should be glad to know whether there is any Hopes of getting some of our Country Party returned among the sixteen.

Your Lordship sees the Numbers of our County Election in the News-papers but I must let you know the reason how Mr. Chester came to be so far before my son. In the first place when we set out last year he was thought so far behind that we took all the Pains we could to set him forwards, and afterwards Stephens either out of Policy, or out of Pique to me, threw all the Votes he could upon Mr. Chester, and turned several who had promised my son either to vote single for himself, or give their second Votes to Mr. Chester; besides which we find about 2 or 300 voted single for Mr. Chester upon some mistaken notion or other, but as it happened my son had still a Majority of 654 and it would have been made up 700 if we had not closed the Poll. I beg pardon for troubling your Lordship with this long account but we are very proud of our Victory, it being to be observed that there have not been two Torys sent up out of this County not ever since the Revolution, and only 2 or 3 instances that one has got in.

note.value: FROM RICHARD WARDMAN TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: York, May 18, 1734.
My Lord,
We are now in great hopes of crowning our desire for Sir Miles Stapylton. I shall set down hear underneath this line how the poul stud Friday night.

It is now thought that it is out of all their power to hinder Sir Miles to be the very first man chose for this election, and the next too him we think will bee ether Mr. Turner or Mr. Wortley without they deceive us with some unknown men. My Lord Milton interest I fancy has not answered his expectation, for his number of men has made but a poor show, and indeed his way of making interest was with employing a parcel of attorneys that loved both money and wine more then serving him; and if Sir Rowland Win loose the poule I may say it will bee a great grief to both Lord and Lady Milton. They appear hear with two coaches, all their childer and all their servants, all new close, new furniture, and cost a great and rare show.
My Lord Downs brought in 700 men
Hazelbee of Rippen brought in 1700 men
Duncome and some joined him 600 men
Lord Strafford and Wentworth Woley 600 men
Lord Strafford and Wortley 600 men
Bamforth near Shefield 200 men

I have not time before the post goes to say any more, but those that I have mentioned is all for Sir Miles' interest, and it is thought, this day being Saturday, that before night it will bee near known who will get the better; though they must bee nice judges to find out the other party seceritts, for they carry every thing so close that we live in fear till such times as it is over. I shall give your lordship a better account by Sunday post; and I wanted to let your lordship known how
we stud this Saturday at noon, but their harts fales them, we have so many men to be poled and they very few, that they will not cast up their books.

note.value: FROM RICHARD WARDMAN TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: York, May 20, 1734.
My Lord,

I hope this day will put us in great hopes of making us sure of Sir Miles being the very first man elected, though a great many thinks that he will not, but Sir Miles and Sir John Blown dus not at tall fear it. As yesterday was Sunday I have been riding about Wakefield and all the placess where I thought I cud do any serviss.
Sir Miles voters of Saturday night 6428
Turner 5598
Win 5554
Mr. Wortley 4864

Sir Miles is before them all 830 men, and they do think that Mr. Wortley will out poul Sir Rowland Win. It is this day at 12 a clock thought that it will bee Sir Miles and Mr. Turner; but God knows what men they have yeet to come, for just now as I was writing this letter hear is 800 men coming in for Turner and Win, which puts a stop to our thoughts. Mr. Wortley is very much commended for his behavever, and if it bee possible they will bring him in, for the Cetty of York gives all their vots to Sir Miles and Wortley.

note.value: FROM RICHARD WARDMAN TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: York, May 22, 1734.
My Lord,

Never was such an election as this, for we cannot make an end of it I doubt this day. We have been night and day a riding for voters, and just now we have got the better of them; and the number of voters stands thus -
Sir Miles Stapylton is 7899
Wortley is 5901
Win is 7702
Turner is 7877

So it certainly will be Sir Miles and Turner which all the world of our side will bee very well pleased. They have just now shut up their Books, but it is sopos'd that the other side will have a screwteney and are very hot upon it, but Mr. Wortley stands to Sir Miles and backs him out bravely; but what the consequence will bee at last I cannot tell at present, for all the gentlemen that is Sir Mileses friends is desired to stay by him to the last pinch, and indeed every body that is Sir Miles friends has been very active, for it has been the hottest election that ever was in England.

Your lordship interest and Mr. Wortley has spoiled my Lord Malton's, that he cud not nor did not bring in by a great number they expected , which I believe has been a great grief to my Lord Milton and Lady Milton, and it is said that Sir Rowland Win Lady frets very much now. My Lord Bruce is in the town, Mr. Duncome, Mr. Heazellbe, Mr. Wentworth of Woley, and twenty more I do not know, who dus not spare money nor man nor horse; as likewise on the other side my Lord Milton has taken as much pains and come every day to the Grand jury room, but this day he has not comed, for he feared all was over.

note.value: FROM RICHARD WARDMAN TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Wentworth Castle, May 24, 1734.
My Lord,

I got home last Wedinsday night, God be thanked, and am alive and my poor mare, I doubt I have almost kilt her; and two horses we borrowed, one of John Crawshaw, one of Tomey Walker, and they have broke both their backs and I doubt will both die. Sir Miles has had the honer of being the very first man chose at this great election, and was carried in the chare about York. He outpouled Mr. Turner 17 men and Sir Rowland 109 men, which is a very great affliction to my Lord Milton, and Sir Rowland wants to have a screwtaney; but I hope they will consider better of it and will let it end with nine nights wonder. When their hot blud is cooled once they will consider that they will bee in the ronge, or at least will consider that money will grow cost.

My charges will come to about 4 or 5 pounds, and if these
two horses die, it will make the journey so much dearer. I cannot tell what Mr. Traviss has spent, but he has lost his horse, he was stole I believe out of the stable the first night, and I left him at York in a sad freat. Their was three horses kilt or died one night at York. Mr. Wortley tenants has two horses by us that is almost dead, but this is owing too carelessness. I lent two of your lordship's old horses, and sent them to grass at Streethousess, where they was well taken care off, and is no worse at tall.

I have found your lordship's letter dated the 14th instant, and you mention that if Sir Miles looses the election you will be railed at, and if he caryes it your lordship expects no great thanks; but I cannot think no such thing, for Sir Miles was pleased to see us, both Mr. Travis and me, and I am sure I took as much pains as any man, and rid to Wakefield all night and fetched up all the old men I cud git; and indeed so did everybody that was concerned, and if we had not been so very active as we wear we had lost the day. Mr. Phipps he hopt about and told every body Mr. Wortley would come in before Sir Rowland; and I will do him justice that if any body axed what number your lordship sent in, he cracked and lied well enough, and so did Mr. Travis, so that nobody did know how meney or how few we had. I cannot say but your lordship will come pretty well of, and if you had joined any of them more money had gon, and would not have looked no better then what your lordship did by sending Travis and me; and as we have got in Sir Miles their no danger but he will return his thanks to every body at his proper time, and so farewell elections.

note.value: FROM GEORGE PHIPPS TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My noble Lord,

Mr. Wortley went from York to Newcastle, and he is not returned, but I expect him in'a week or less. Sir Miles was att Leeds Races, and was upon a scaffold, and gentlemen crowding upon it the scaffold shot an end, but going gradually down no person was hurt except two men that was below.

Lord Milton went to Milton, and his Lady, on Friday after the poll ended; and returned on Thursday morning, when the Sheriff declared Sir Miles and Turner. I think Lord M- got home the 1st inst., or night before; but I think Lady M- never stopped in York in their way from Milton, or att least if she did she never appeared, that I could see; as I wrote before, Lord Milton was in town but never appeared att the windows as usual in the great room att the George Inn. If Rowland and Turner had carried their point there was to have been fine balls, and venison to be sent from Woodhouse; and then have took a tour to Scarborough. There was one or two of their creatures had patched up little equipages for that purpose, but we spoiled their dancing, &c. and at last Sir Ro- or Lord M-, or both are to pay the piper without dancing, for as I am told,
and I am satisfied it is so, they agreed to pay Mr. Turner all the expense he sho'd be att if in case Turner would join Sir Ro-. I take that to be the chief motive of Turner joining Sir Rowland.

Lord M-, I am told for certain by his workman that as soon as he got home turned of all his workmen except Mark Smith, and a few of other sorts of workmen who are finishing the bargains. We have a neighbour's daughter, who Lady Ma- turned away last Thursday; the girl says that another servant informed Lady Ma- that she joined in the cry att York (a Stapleton for ever), and the girl said when she went out of the house she said to one of the servants, now she would cry 'Stapleton for ever.' The girl says that Lady Ma- bought a fine suite of clothes, but, loosing the election, the close was never unpacked and her ladyship's Scarbrough journey was put off. The girl says that for some time past her ladyship has pleased herself with the thoughts of a petition being lodged next Sessions; but such a thing would make Lord Ma- more ridiculous and hated then he is. The girl I spoke of was att Milton with Lady M-, and what vexed her ladyship very much was, the mob all the road to Milton and those voters which had been att York affronted them all the way "Down with the Rump, no bull beef, a Stapleton and Wortley for ever." Tic said that Mr. Westby of Ranfield left Lord Milton att York upon some words; Lord M- was so ill vexed that he stuck att nothing, so Mr. Westby did not altogether like his going on, upon which spoke his opinion which Lord M- did not like, so parted in a civil way as it is said. Mr. Griffith has complained against the housekeeper and the steward at Woodhouse for not treating the freeholds as they shoud have done; so they both are in disgrace. They say Lord Milton is very much out of temper and sower. Sir William Rooke is gone mad upon this election; Mr. Witton is very much disordered; one Doctor Lee of Divinity of Halifax is disordered; and Coll. Folly behaves himself very oddly. They are like people just awaked from a dream, they can scarce believe the election is lost, they made themselves so
sure of it. Lord Milton is very much vexed att bonfires which are made att every little town round about; never such bonfires and rejoyceing I never see upon any occasion, and people gives money to drink. It is reported Turner is dead, but I can't affirm it; but, if so, Mr. Wortley will out poll Sir Rowland 1000 men.

note.value: FROM PETER WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Kensington, September 20, 1734.
Dear Brother,

Since I received the enclosed letter I send you from George, Mr. Carew arrived here, and I have been several times in his company, and he give me the pleasure to assure me that George is really become a sober diligent young fellow, and sticks close to P. Max. where ever he goes, and keeps the colours vacant for him, but does not give him the commission, because he would still keep him near his person; as soon as he has it the rest of the officers will be calling out for his doing duty in his post; and he says in six months he dares swear the P. Max. will give a company when he'll under stand the language better, but says your letter is much expected both to him and Prince Eugene to revite them in their good intention to dear G-; and I have been told by him and several considerable Germains here that letters of recommendations from great men in England is of more service with Germain Generals then a purse of gold, therefore I once more entreat to write to Prince Eugene and Max., and I have and will tell every body it is by my desire you do not yet give him any more then you have given him, till we see further proofs of his good behaviour.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, April 15, 1735.
Dear Papa,

I wish it was in my power to write again with my silver pen since you like it, but I gave it yesterday to Mr.
Godfroy to have my arms engraved on it. He asked me for my arms and coronet 18 pence, but for my supporters he asked me three shillings and sixpence, so you may be sure I would have only my arms for I think quite extravagant to have any thing else; I am overjoyed, for the queen has just sent to invite me to the Duke's ball. I am to go at half an hour after six and I am to be dressed in all my best, and Mr. Morin is sent for to do up my hair, and so I am to go to the Drawing room this morning and to wait of the Duke. I am to dine at Mr. Scawens to day. My momma and sisters goes to night to Mr. Leveridge's benefit, I was to have gone had not the Duke sent. Mr. Scawen got them her, for he makes great interest for him, the play is the Royal merchant or the beggars bush with a vast deal of dancing and Mr. Glover and Madameselle Salle.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, May 27, 1735.
Dear Papa,

We are all to dine at the dowager Lady Burlington's to-day, I fancy there will be a great feast. My Lady Swasso is dead, she deyed in a convulsion fit as she was at dinner with a great deal of company, it was in the news yesterday. We dined yesterday at Lady Francis Williams, my mama and I; the company was Lady Coningsby, Lady Francis Williams, my mama, fat Lord Hinton, tall Mr. Selwin, and Mr. Williams and I. We had a very good dinner, for we had at the first course three macerell, then after that we had beans and bacon and boiled chikens, and then we had four little plates pigeons one rabbits , in an other goosberry tart and sparrow grase and no desert. I think I have told you all the news I know, so I will tire you no longer with stupid letter.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: St. James's Square, June 3, 1735.

note.value: PASSAGE OMITTED

text.p: I was at Kingsington a Sunday, there was a good deal of company, and the Queen very civil. I hired a mare and Lucy and I went in your machine chariot, Lady Anne carred Lady Gallway and Mrs. Candish in her coach, but we went and cam together. Lord Bathurst cam here the other morning and told me I might know the viset was to my self, for he knew you was out of town. He cam between one and two and stayed till past three. He has a most extrordinary fancy for a conveyance at Cirencester that outdoes your contrivances, but I am sure I would not go in it; he designs to buy the bottom of an old barge that holds twelve people, and to put it upon the carredg of a waggon, and so to have it drawn about with six horses, and a table in the middle. I find he sees Lady Suffolk often.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Cirencester, August 11, 1735.
My Dear Lord,

Your Lordship's letter followed me down here, and I had the Pleasure of receiving it the day after I arrived. I cannot easily tell you the great satisfaction it gave me, to find my self in your thoughts, to find that you and all your family are now in good health, and as appeared by your letter full of spirits and cheerful; I received only one mortification from it, that I can have no hopes this year of enjoying your good company in that agreeable place. As I am but just got hither your Lordship may easily imagine that I have a great many things to doe, the summer will be over before I have looked round me. I unfortunately engaged in an affair of selling one Estate and buying another just as the Parliament rose, imagining I might have finished all the matter in 3
weeks time; one delay upon the back of another kept me in town till the latter end of the last week. Your Lordship who is a lover of the Country may judge of the mortification it was to me to be kept so long away from a Place I am fond off, and confined to a Place I dislike extremely at this time of year. My health has suffered by it, and I own my self at present many years older than your Lordship, for I am sure by your last letter that you are quite in health and Vigour.

Your Lordship need not recommend to me the laying aside all Political thoughts. I was sufficiently tired with the wild schemes and Conjectures of the Politians I used to meet in the Park I shall scarce look into a news paper for these next two months. I am already laying designs for the next season's planting and that will take up all my thoughts till I am obliged to come to town again. I make use of that expression for I really look upon it as an obligation for every person who has a seat in Parliament to attend during the Session, at least whilst there is any hopes that a Vote may be of use; I am not yet convinced but it may be of Use, and even in the next Session of Parliament. We still enjoy more liberty than some other Countries. I have read in an account of Persia that when the Eunuchs governed there as sole Ministers they made the Sophie publish an Edict to forbid the people from making Capons, the privilege of - being reserved for themselves, and too great an Honour to be communicated to Brutes; now we have still the liberty of cutting our Fowls, and I believe under the present gentle administration might be admitted to - ourselves; a benefit I ought in Prudence to have taken hold off some years ago, that I might not have got more Children than I am now able to maintain, considering the just and necessary taxes we are all obliged to pay to support the Exigencies of the Government who have laboured under a long and fruitless Peace.

But, my Dear Lord, if I can get rid of a cruel Head-ach which has persecuted me this last week, I shall trouble my self about nothing, but receive the joy of hearing of my Friends when they are absent, and keeping my self in hopes of seeing them in Health and Spirits next winter. Your
Lordship may be assured you are always uppermost in my thoughts, being sincerely with the utmost regard and Esteem, &c.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Bruton? February 14, 1736.
My Lord,

After a thousand acknowledgments for your unwearyed goodness, give me leave to say I am unjustly complained of, for with what face can I without absolute necessity trouble my nearest friends with letters from such a place as you know this is. Though I never stir, it is a pleasure to hear of your motions, because I believe they preserve your health. My Lady Westmerland I have known ever since I was her neighbour in Dover street and remember dining with her in your Lordship's green house at Twitnam; but My Lady Kildare is a much longer acquaintance, your Lordship very justly remarks her great politeness and entertaining conversation, but perhaps you do not know that it is never at the cost of any body she lives with at all civilly; in this she is strict to a scruple. My Lord Poulet I visit once in a summer, I doe not hear he stirs in matters of election. He is constantly kind to me; his son I know but little. I may truly say a day seldom passes without my remembering your kind visit here, in a humour that left me no room for wishes, unless it were for lengthening that happiness. I have sent for the pamphlet that is so much in vogue, tho I read but few, unless well recommended as this is. I don't know how it is in other places, but where I am concerned no tenants pay, and we must live upon air, though moist and unpleasant with the continual rains.
The entertaining letter I have now before me cures all present uneasynesses and I am with the greatest truth &c.

note.value: FROM ANNE, LADY STRAFFORD TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Tusday, 4 o'clock .

We are my Dearest just com from Court where there was really a great deal of finery. The Princess is neither handsome nor ugly, tall nor short, but has a lively pretty countenance enough. The D. of Grafton told me we ware to meet in the Great Drawing room at six, and the Peers and Peeress's to eithere go down into the Chaple after the Queen, or to sit during the Ceremony above in the King's closet (which he said as a friend he thought would be the best place). Then we are to see them supp and then see them abed; and tomorrow at twelve o'clock we are to go to be presented in the Princess's room, and at night is a ball.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: My Dear Lord,

I would not have troubled you with a letter singly to have made my Compliments to you and returned you my thanks for the Honour you have done me, but I am really in pain till I hear how you got to the Bath, and what alteration you find in your health there. Your Lordship had a terrible day for the journey, but I think the thunder and Rain have cooled the Air a little, which will make the Place you are in more supportable, and the Waters more Beneficial.

If you stay a fortnight, I can't help coming over to look at you for one day, in hopes of prevailing with you to give me one day at least upon the return, and one day when you are in health will be better than a week whilst you are in disorder, nay I will fairly own to you, in your last visit you gave more pain than pleasure to your obedient and faithful servant.
I beg my compliments to Lady Strafford and Lord Wentworth.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Cirencester, July 17, 1736.
My Dear Lord,

I hope this will overtake you and find you safely arrived at Wentworth Castle. I don't think any Air is so good as that where a Man of taste has laid out his works himself; there is certainly more pleasure in riding about woods which have been cut and modelled by one's own contrivance and fancy, and through Avenues of one's own planting than in any others what soever, and as pleasure tends to health I think your Lordship is more likely to find benefit by that than by all Dr. Cheney's prescriptions. However I please my self with this reflection, I should be glad to have it certified under your own hand, or under Lord Wentworth's, who without any disparagement to you certainly writes a better: Indeed he writes too well for a Man of Quality, but I comfort my self that when he comes into the world and has been an Ambassador and Plenipotentiary abroad, or a Secretary of State at home, the delicacy of his hand-writing will go off; till then I am ashamed to write to him, for mine is good for nothing and yet I have never had any business to spoil it.

I can assure you my Lord I shall go on with much more satisfaction with my plain works now since they have had some share of your approbation, and if you would be so good as to come and see them once every year you would spur me on to do something handsome. The truth of it is I have undertaken too large a design for my pocket and I must leave to a son or a Grand-son to finish. I can imagine what it will be 50 or 60 year hence and the force of my imagination must supply the weakness of my purse.

Your Lordship has the Pleasure of seeing things almost in perfection in your own time, a noble building and plantations well grown about it, but the most agreeable sight you can see there is that fine youth who is one time or other to succeed you in it. Without any compliment I like him better the more I see of him and I really think he promises every thing that can be desired. My best wishes will always attend your Lordship and him, but I must not conclude without making my compliments
to my Lady Strafford, and my wife tells me we ought to make many excuses for the ill entertainment we gave her here, but I tell her that neither My Lady nor your Lordship came here to be entertained within doors, and it was the fault of the weather and your Lordship's indisposition which hindered me from entertaining you better without; however without making excuses I trust to your Lordship's goodness to excuse all faults and omissions in one who is so sincerely &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: Cirencester, September 6, 1736.

If I calculate right My Dear Lord you must have been now about a week at Wentworth Castle, and before this letter comes to your hands you will have had a fortnight's rest there, and trial of the Effect the Scarborough Waters have had upon you. Now I beg of your Lordship most earnestly that in a post or two after you receive this, you will order a servant to write me in two or three lines an exact account of the state
of your health, and then afterwards at you own leisure you will send me an answer to this.

I am in great hopes those waters, the bathing in the sea, and the Exercise may have totally re-establish'd your health. I think all the three have an equal chance to be of service in your case; but if these Rheumatic complaints and want of sleep should still remain I hope your Lordship will resolve to go to London for advise without delay. I am persuaded Dr. Burton would cure you. It is plain that your Lordship's disorder is from the Blood and Juices, that is to be rectified by proper Medicines. Your Lordship ought not to be reckoned above 50 year old. I seriously think you are as young as I am, considering the difference of Natural Strength; and if I had the same complaints as you have, I should make no doubt of getting rid of them by a Course of Medicine under Dr. Burton's care in 6 weeks time; I name that period, because I have heard him and other Physicians say that in such a space they can entirely change the habit of the Body in respect to the Blood and Juices.

I hope you will be in a condition to laugh at all this advice which I have the impertinence to send you. I shall be exceedingly glad to find that, but if it should prove otherwise (which God forbid) I then most earnestly beg of you to follow it without delay, for delay may so totally alter the habit of your Body that it may be incurable. I know you hate Physic and Physicians and love Quacks, but I should think that you have suffered enough by them to grow wiser for the future; I am satisfied that Ward poisoned you, and if the effects of it are not yet quite recovered it is high time to consult with those who can remove them. I am very serious upon this affair and therefore write with that freedom which becomes a friend, a Relation, and an humble servant, upon a serious occasion. It is a rainy day and therefore my thoughts are more gloomy, and I shall remain under apprehensions of your indisposition's hanging upon you till I am assured of the contrary.

It is a very sickly time all about us, but my family continue well at present. I go on with my works and have great
satisfaction in hoping to see your Lordship here next year and show you quite a new scene about the House. I have cut throw one of the Hills and let in a View up one of the Diagonals which terminates upon a little building which I have erected; next summer I shall build another to answer the other Diagonal and cut through that Hill, and by removing part of the Hill before the House in the straight line I shall have a View of the Park which I propose to set off a little with some proper Ornaments. All this levelling work will not amount to above 50 or 60 l. and the situation of the House will appear as good again as it does at present. I have brought a considerable quantity of stone and laid it round that stand in the great Centre of my wood, that when some unskillfull person sees it, he may be convinced that wooden machine was not erected with a design to remain, but only for a trial to see what height and size would be proper for the stone-building; having done this I may let my stone lie there as long as Lord Bristol has left his for the building of his House. I waited upon My Lord Chancellor Talbot a little time ago who has a pretty place about 12 miles off, but a sad House, and finds himself obliged to build. He has not begun yet, he has very good stone near him but he is so surrounded with Common fields that I think he cant possibly make a great thing of it, but it may be made a pretty thing. The Park may be made like yours at Boughton and he has a pretty river runs by one side of it. It is just such a kind of place which I believe your Lordship will agree with me can't possibly make a noble seat, like Wentworth Castle, Castle Howard, &c. My Lord Chancellor is very fond of sports, and he has a fine Country about him for that purpose.

Having nothing more to send your Lordship from hence I shall only beg leave to make my Compliments to Lady Strafford the young Ladies and Lord Wentworth, and I beg your Lordship to tell him that if he likes hunting he must come here to see it in perfection; you have nothing like it in Yorkshire except upon the Wolds, which is too far from you. I'm sure I could entertain him here in the hunting-season to his satisfaction.
Adieu My Dear Lord and be assured that I am with the Utmost sincerity respect and affection &c.

note.value: FROM ALLEN, LORD BATHURST TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD
RECEIVED OCTOBER 18, 1736

text.p: My Dear Lord,

I have omitted for some time to return your Lordship my thanks for your last obliging letter, having had company in the House with me and a good deal of business besides. It gave me great satisfaction to find that your Lordship was so far recovered; but I tremble to think of the strange way of managing yourself, to bath in the sea contrary to the advise of your Physician, and when your blood was so much disordered that you found you wanted a fire when other people complained of heat; to travel about afterwards with a violent looseness upon you, to stop that all at once without any precaution; a thing which has killed a hundred men, and you come off with a fit of the Gout for 24 hours. Indeed My Lord you have too good a Constitution to be thrown away at this rate. You want nothing but to rectify your Blood after having been poisoned by Ward's Arsenic, and you have at least 10 years to come of youth and Vigour. Now what I would beg of your Lordship is this; to leave the Country and come up to town, unless you find you are perfectly recovered, and then to put your self into the hands of Dr. Burton, who is both an understanding man and an honest man; I dare answer for it that he would set you up in as good order as you ever were in your life, and then for God's sake resolve never to meddle with Quacks again as long as you live. I hope your Lordship will forgive me for pretending to give you advise, I would not be so bold upon any other occasion; If I err, it is in thinking your health of greater consequence than you doe your self, and as I really think I have a great concern in it, as well as every body else must have who has the honour to know you, I can't forgive you for managing it so ill.

I wish I could have the pleasure of waiting on you at Wentworth Castle but I can't at present stir from hence and
if I should be obliged to go to my own affairs in those parts it will be towards Christmas by which time your Lordship will certainly be removed to London. I am determined however to pay my respects to you there next year if I am able; I think of making my tour as soon as the Parliament is up, and I don't see anything likely to happen which should occasion a long sessions.

My wife desires to be joined with me in making our Compliments to my Lady Strafford Lord Wentworth and the young Ladies and I will trouble your Lordship no further but to beg leave to assure you that I am with the utmost sincerity and respect,
Your Lordship's most faithful and obedient servant
Bathurst.

note.value: FROM LADY LUCY WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, January 8, 1737.
Dear Papa,

My mama has been so good to give me leave to go to the Opera to night with Lady Anne. It is to be a new one called Meropy, but the foolish Buffo's are to be left out which I am very glad of, but am sorry they are to have five hundred pound a piece for acting that silly stuf two nights, if one may believe Mr. Hamilton. The Opera is to be heard but once for he says it is the worst that ever was composed. Lady Anne was last wensday at Mr. Handle's house and she likes the new man much better then Conte'
who she does not at all approve of. We were very sorry the Queen would not keep Twelf night, I believe nobody regretted more then I, except the Groom Porter, who I hear is much disturbed about it, tho to comfort us both her majesty says when the King comes she'll make a Twelf night, which I don't credit much. We were at court last night, and Miss Chambers was the finest body, but I can't say the handsomest. Lord Tulimoor seemed to have a mind for her, but Mr. Grenvill soon came and displaced him. The most unhappy body I know is Miss Clavering who was married yesterday to my Lord Donkelan, for I never heard any man have so bad a character; he has lately almost killed his servant, they don't think he can live. I had a letter yesterday from Lady Anne Wentworth, but she said Yorkshire was just as we left it, and no news stirring but Miss Fuljamb's wedding, which she gave me no other particulars but that Mr. Ebetson had given her a fine watch set with diamonds. I hope, Dear Papa, you wont take it ill that I writ so much (considering how dull it is) for nothing would make me more unhappy, since the whole study of my life will be in every respect how to please your Lordship and to prove how sincerely I am as I ought to be Dear Papa
Your most affectionate and most dutiful daughter
L. Wentworth.
Lady Hariot begs her duty to your Lordship.

note.value: FROM WILLIAM, LORD BERKELEY OF STRATTON TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: January 12, 1737.

Give me leave My Lord a little to unburden my heart and reproach you for coming so near without letting me know it. If you did not care to see me, I commend your prudence, for I would certainly have gone to the Bath, at least for one night, as I did since to see an acquaintance. This mortification was succeeded by another, when I heard you were not well, but I hope it was a false report, or that you are well
recovered, since your assembly is in the prints. One line will dispel my black vapours. You are a long time without the sun shine of his Matie. One would think some witch raised these cross winds, as K. James the first thought when kept in Denmark and hanged several after his return to Scotland. One side of paper is enough from this retired corner. May you long live happy and kind to your most obedient servant.

note.value: FROM LADY LUCY WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, January 18, 1737.
Dear Papa,

I fear this will prove a very short Epistle there being nothing now to be heard of but the King, which no body knows so much of as your self, your civilities was not at all lost for it is every body's conversation how much obliged his majesty was to you, and he looked with quite a pleased face on the whole family, which did not always happen. There's vast crowds every day to be presented, and every body at court looks happy. Last Sunday there was a vast deal of music at Church, too much I think, for I doubt it spoilt every body's devotion, for there was drums and Trumpits as loud as an Oritoria. I wish the news may be true about Lady Russel's money that is found. I own I think if there's as much found as will pay her debts her relations has done very ill by her, not to be more careful in searching before they let her memory be so exposed. Lord Persival is to be married soon; she's to have twenty Thousand pound, and Lord Egmont is to allow 'em in present 1500 l. a year and their house in Pell-mell. It is now said there'll certainly be a night at Court for play and a ball as of Twelf day. I was very sorry to see the whether so bad as it was yesterday for it must make the country very unpleasant but to day is charming fine, we have not walked once I think since you went. I wonder you don't name Mr. Tyrell for I fancied he'd be a sure visitor for you oftener perhaps then you could wish. They have begun to act the Buffo's again and I believe will perform before his majesty to
night for the first time, for he was not at the Opera a saturday as most people thought he would to show he was safely arrived. Tho it is with great pleasure I write Yet I wish to doe it no more having hopes that before my Dear Papa can receive a another of my letters I may in person assure him, I am, with great sincerity his
most Affectionate and most Dutiful Daughter
L. Wentworth.

note.value: FROM LADY LUCY WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, January 29, 1737.

Most people when they write wish their letter to be received, but I differ from them now for I hope my Dear Papa wont get this, but will have left Free-stone before this arrives there. Mr. Conolly was here this morning and desired his duty to you and wishes your hops may prosper, but is sorry you had not Taffy to assist you. As Lord Vane has taken so much pains to get my Lady and as it is in so particular a way I thought you would not dislike to see the Advertisement so I've sent it, as I knew you have it not in any of your news-papers. I never thought I shoud have vanity enough to Imagine I could Rivel my Dear Papa in any thing, but I really think I stand a fare chance for it now in Lady Kildare's favour for she invited me to spend the evening with her last Saturday which I did, and at parting our Compliments were so long that my Cousin Hanbury (who was to carry me home) thought she shoud have dyed with laughing, or rather the fears of staying there all night. Lady Pen Cholmondly is come to town but where she is I cant tell. Sr Tho. Franklin's Daughter's match is quite at an end upon some Ill behaviour of Mr. Boucher's. Lady Andover is come to town and the greatest beauty that has been seen a great while; they are to live on with Lord Berkshire. Lord Tankervill has now a great mind to be friends with my Lady and says if she'll live with him again he'll give her a new suit of Close - but I fancy she wont sell her quiet at so cheap a rate. I had a letter from Mrs. Ebetson who says her father is a most
dismal widower, I am not at all surprised at it (for I always thought him a most dismal stupid man). Lady Anne desires her duty to your Lordship and thanks you vastly for the hare which was a very fine one; Lady Hariot also desires her duty and I hope Dear Papa will doe me the Justice to believe I am with the utmost truth his
Most Affectionate and most Dutiful Daughter.

note.value: FROM LADY LUCY WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, December 29, 1737.

Tho it is always a sincere pleasure to me to write to my Dear Papa yet I own when I considered I had nothing in the world to say it mortified me extremely till I reflected I was to dine at Lady Key's and then I thought if I stayed till I came home, I could not fail of producing some news, but I find I have stayed for little purpose. We had a very gentle pretty dinner, and her gentleman very well dressed; she was very sorry you was not of the party. She told us of Lady Kenoul's good luck; somebody spoke in her favour to the Queen just before she dyed, but the goodness she intended her was by her majesty's death prevented, but now it has been told the King, he said he was sensible by not knowing Lord Oxford much he had not behaved to him so well as he deserved, but he hoped to make him some amends by immediately ordering Lady Kenoul a pension of 600 l. a year, and to be paid her and my lord to have nothing to doe with it. She's coming up to town to return the King her thanks. It is thought their won't be any settled drawing rooms till the twelf day and new years day is over, because the King chooses to avoid seeing so much company as are always at court on those days. Lord Vane keeps a Lady in the country, so he's now easy without my Lady, but she's coming to town from the Bath, and says she's sure she can behave in a manner that will make her be esteemed as well as ever. Poor Lady Kay has got all her trumperys together to be ready to wait on the Prince and Princess a sunday, but I fancy, though she'll spare no pains, she'll hardly rival Lady Archibald. If this frosty weather continues I conclude you'll make your visits on foot to Lady Anne Hervy, but I doubt she'll never return
them in the same manner to you. Lady Helena Perceval is to spend the evening with us and is here already, but I hope my Dear Papa will doe me the justice to believe no bodies company can give me half the pleasure that I feal when I can asure him how much I am with the greatest regard his Lordships most affectionate and most dutiful daughter.

note.value: FROM LADY LUCY WENTWORTH TO THOMAS WENTWORTH, EARL OF STRAFFORD

text.p: London, January 3, 1738.
Dear Papa,
